pistons.headline: The Pistons go from owning to getting owned in the paint
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 04: Jalen Duren #0 of the Detroit Pistons looks on from the bench during a game against the Philadelphia 76ers at Little Caesars Arena on November 04, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

During a tumultuous playoff run and a prolonged offseason contract negotiation, Detroit Pistons fans were ready to say goodbye to Jalen Duren. Well, Duren has been out for six of eight games, and it turns out that Duren is the most indispensable member of the Pistons aside from Cade Cunningham.

A hamstring strain has knocked Duren out for six straight and counting, and boy, do you feel that every moment of every Pistons game.

Pundits and fans alike had easy diagnoses for what ailed the 60-win team during a disappointing second-round exit last season. Detroit needed a second scorer and much more perimeter shooting to succeed in the postseason. Its second-best player, the All-NBA big man Duren, couldn’t effectively operate in a congested, constipated offense when opponents had so much extra time to prepare their defense. That had a trickle-down effect on Cade Cunningham and on offensively limited players the Pistons relied on, like Ausar Thompson, Javonte Green, and Ron Holland.

This offseason, the Pistons seemingly tried and failed to add their second scorer (a planned run at Austin Reaves fizzled, and trade interest in players such as Kyrie Irving and Kevin Durant went nowhere). But they certainly addressed the team’s lack of perimeter punch. Detroit added guys such as Isaiah Joe, John Collins, and Taurean Prince. They re-signed midseason acquisition Kevin Huerter. They reformulated their offensive game plan to create more movement, space, and offensive responsibility among their non-Cade players. So far this season, the perimeter offense has hummed. Detroit is a top-10 team in 3-point shooting and almost middle of the pack in attempts despite Isaiah Joe missing most of the season to injury.

Detroit is 6-2, losing to the New York Knicks and on Wednesday night to the East-leading Philadelphia 76ers. Calls after both games from fans and casual watchers immediately turn to the team’s lack of that second star as the biggest issue. While that still might be a deal-breaker in the players, I would argue that the actual biggest issue in the season’s first eight games is Detroit’s collapse in its former ability to absolutely own the paint.

In other words, it’s not the lack of a Kyrie or a Durant or a Devin Booker. It’s the lack of Duren.

Last season, Detroit led the NBA in points in the paint, mostly behind Duren’s elite rim gravity and chemistry with Cade Cunningham and Detroit’s other ball handlers. Last season, the Pistons led the NBA with 57.9 points in the paint and were fourth in opponents’ paint scoring. They had a scoring differential inside of 14.2 points per game.  This season, Detroit ranks just 22nd in the paint at 44.8, down 13.1 points per game.

Rim gravity, it turns out, is just as important as perimeter shooting in creating the space needed to run a successful offense.

Paul Reed is a dynamic scorer inside, and he has some pop to his game. But he isn’t a rim runner like Duren. You give it to him on the block, and you let him work his magic. John Collins is opportunistic in transition, but those opportunities are dried up when he is the only big on the floor applying rim pressure, usually trying to duck in from the corners.

Ausar has the ball in his hands more, and it is working to create opportunities from others on the perimeter, but it is taking away a lot of those dunker-spot opportunities and back cuts that Thompson feasted on last season.

The lack of inside pressure is manifesting in other ways. Detroit has gone from a top-5 team in second-chance points to 22nd. They are 28th in offensive rebounding. Last season, they were third.

This team needs Jalen Duren back ASAP. And I think fans need to start reckoning with how crucial he is for this team to succeed.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs 76ers final score: Detroit falls short in East battle
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 04: Cade Cunningham #2 of the Detroit Pistons drives around Vj Edgecombe #77 of the Philadelphia 76ers during the first half at Little Caesars Arena on November 04, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Pistons (6-2) fall short in the battle between the top teams in the Eastern Conference. The Philadelphia 76ers (8-1) outlasted Detroit 112-106. Philly got up by as many as 18 points, but Detroit never truly went away. The 76ers’ stardom showed its head tonight.

After holding Jaylen Brown to 16 points in the first meeting of the season, he surpassed that in the first half this time around. Brown poured in 30 points for the game while converting on 11 of his 19 shots. He rained in spot-up 3s, as it was tough to stick with him with the way Philly forced Detroit into scramble mode throughout the ballgame. Brown had a clutch block on Cade, and his presence was felt on both sides of the ball.

This is not 2023 Joel Embiid, but he’s still a force. Embiid still draws double teams and can get any big in foul trouble. He and Tolu Smith got into a dust-up that injected some life into Detroit, but Philly found a way to withstand every Detroit storm.

Duncan Robinson went on a few personal runs that seemed to turn the tide in Detroit’s favor. The sharpshooter went for 27 points and buried an unconscious seven triples. Robinson’s ability to look past the hands in his face to shoot the rock will pay dividends all season. It didn’t work out tonight, but Robinson is off to a different type of start as a sniper.

Cade Cunningham tried to put on his cape and emptied the clip. He couldn’t find it from deep but got good looks. He went for 26 points, 11 assists, and seven boards. He got to the charity stripe and nailed every attempt (7-7). Cade had another LeBron-like chasedown block — this time in LeBron’s presence.

At this point, those are truly Cade-like chasedowns, and Brown’s missed layup here shows Cade’s reputation as a chasedown artist is evident.

Jaylen Brown misses the wide open layup. 😬 pic.twitter.com/jMyfS41RJG
— Hoop Central (@TheHoopCentral) November 5, 2026

VJ Edgecombe had a fast break sequence where he u-turned it because Cade was on the hunt again. Special defender.

Ausar Thompson’s special stuff came on the boards as he snagged 17 rebounds tonight. From the opening possession, he was pogo-sticking down low to help Paul Reed and John Collins in the paint. AT chipped in 11 points, and his shot from the line continues to look better. He was 3-for-4 tonight; you’ll take the small improvements wherever you can.

John Collins had his best offensive game in a few games. He was getting behind the defense, throwing down head-top slams. His ability to be a paint finisher and hit threes is why he’s here. He only shot one 3 tonight. The Pistons need more.

Collins should look better when Duren comes back, in theory. Duren has rim-gravity that forces defenses to account for one of the best finishers in basketball. This was the first game where I thought Detroit missed Duren badly. From a talent perspective, Detroit was outgunned tonight.

LeBron James controlled the tempo in spurts of the game. He was playing like that OG at the Y who’s keeping up with the youngins on pure know-how. LeBron draws two to the ball, Embiid does, Brown does, and Tyrese Maxey does. There’s a lot of star power over there, and this is a team Detroit could see in the long run.

The Pistons did not have their sharpest defensive night, and Philly still only cracked 112. It was just one of the games. Detroit shifts their focus to another superstar in Luka Dončić. He and the Los Angeles Lakers travel to Detroit on Sunday as the Pistons take on their first Western Conference team of the season.

The Detroit Pistons are looking to keep the good times rolling against the Philadelphia 76ers. Detroit and Philly are the two best teams in the East, and the Pistons have already notched one win against the Sixers this season. In fact, the 106-93 win in October was Detroit’s sixth consecutive victory against Philly. Tonight, they go for lucky No. 7. That loss against the Pistons also happens to be Philadelphia’s lone blemish on the season. In that matchup, the Pistons were without the services of Jalen Duren. It worked out because they were able to rely on the all-around goodness of Paul Reed. It also didn’t hurt that Joel Embiid missed that first matchup to rest.

Tonight, the Pistons will have no such luck. They are still missing All-Star big man Duren, and tonight the Sixers will employ the services of their former MVP in Embiid. While Detroit has been playing amazing basketball, they have been vulnerable down low, and Embiid will be the best interior big man they’ve faced since they lost Duren to a hamstring injury.

One benefit in Detroit’s favor is that this is a nationally televised game on ESPN, and it seems like Cade Cunningham loves to come up big when the lights are brightest for national television. Cunningham is also coming off of perhaps his most dominant performance of the season, scoring 33 points in just 26 minutes of action. If the game against the Hornets was close instead of a 30-point blowout late, if seems like Cunningham could have gone for 45 points.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs 76ers preview:  East’s top two teams square off on National TV
pistons.body:
If you are to believe preseason predictions, this game being a showdown between the East’s top two teams could come as a bit of a surprise.  Pistons fans knew this team would be good, but many talking heads predicted a falloff this season while everybody was on board with the 76ers being one of the best teams in the league.

It shouldn’t come as a surprise that the team that was 1st in the East last season is once again competing for the top seed in the East, but talking heads have to make their money somehow.  ESPN at least had the foresight to pickup this game and you get what should be a very fun early-season showdown between two teams that have only lost one game each.

The 76ers and Pistons have played once this season and the Pistons won, but it is tough to draw any conclusions since both teams were missing a couple of starters.

Game Vitals

Where:  Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, MI
When:  Wednesday, November 4 at 7 pm EST
Watch:  ESPN
Odds:  Detroit (-2.5)

Analysis

The Pistons will be without Jalen Duren and Isaiah Joe, who was already ruled out for this game last night.  The Pistons were missing Jalen Duren in the last matchup between these teams and also Ausar Thompson, who they will have back.  But, Isaiah Joe did suffer the hip injury that is still keeping him out during the 1st quarter of the last matchup, so the Pistons are trading one injured player for another.

With this being a National TV game and the 76ers getting a day of rest, I would suspect that everybody plays for them tonight.  In the last matchup, the 76ers did not have Joel Embiid or VJ Edgecombe, which really put their lack of depth to the test.

Joel Embiid’s size and ability on the glass could become a problem for the Pistons, who will continue to start the undersized Paul Reed and likely use John Collins to back him up.  Without Jalen Duren, rebounding was already going to be a problem, but the Pistons have been able to overcome it during his absence.

In the last matchup, the Pistons were able to contain Tyrese Maxey through 3 quarters before he started hitting shots in the 4th.  It was a bit of shocking development since the Pistons were without Ausar Thompson, but without some of the other stars for the 76ers, they could focus their defense more on stopping Maxey.  The 76ers have a lot of star power, but their biggest offensive threat is arguably Maxey, who can hit shots from anywhere on the court and can use his quickness with the ball to get to where he wants.  I would expect Ausar Thompson to draw the Tyrese Maxey matchup which will allow Cade Cunningham to guard Jaylen Brown since he has the size to keep up with him.

I am not really sure what the Pistons are going to do about the Joel Embiid matchup.  Paul Reed is outsized by him and also can have some issues with fouling and Joel Embiid has made a living off of bating fouls throughout his career.  Paul Reed is going to have to stay disciplined, as I don’t think the Pistons can afford to have heavy minutes of John Collins at center or Tolu Smith.  I have full confidence in the Pistons’ ability to matchup with the rest of the 76ers starting lineup, but the most concern I have is this matchup and it very well could swing the game.

If there is one certainty for the Pistons, it is that Cade Cunningham is difficult to slow down, especially with how he is playing now.  He is coming off a 33 points masterclass against the Charlotte Hornets on Monday in only 27 minutes where he absolutely took over the game and turned a single-digit lead into a 20-plus point blowout.  Cade Cunningham always starts off the season slow, but he seems to be hitting his stride now.  His 3-ball is consistently falling as he is shooting 37% from beyond the arc, which is a significant development for his offensive creation abilities and efficiency.

He is going to have to put together another masterclass if the Pistons want any hope to win this game.  During Jalen Duren’s absence, the Pistons have been able to win games through their high-level defense, but their offense has left a lot to be desired.  With Isaiah Joe out and Duncan Robinson going through a bit of a cold stretch, the Pistons shooting fell off a bit and they went four games in a row scoring 110 points or less.

However, everything seemed to get back on track on Monday against the Hornets, so hopefully that continues.

One player the Pistons are hoping gets back on track is John Collins.  He had his best game as a Piston in the last game against the 76ers and has proceeded to score single-digit points in every game since then.  With Jalen Duren out, he has had to play a lot more center than he was probably planning on playing, but he has also had difficulties finding a consistent offensive role.  Another big John Collins game would be a huge help in this matchup

The Joel Embiid matchup concerns me with the Pistons lack of frontcourt size, but if they can defend Tyrese Maxey like they did in the last matchup, they have a shot to takedown the 76ers and claim the top seed in the Eastern Conference.

Lineups

Detroit Pistons (6-1):  Cade Cunningham, Duncan Robinson, Ausar Thompson, John Collins, Paul Reed

Philadelphia 76ers (7-1):  Tyrese Maxey, VJ Edgecombe, Jaylen Brown, LeBron James, Joel Embiid

Question of the Day

Which of these teams will finish higher in the Eastern Conference at the end of the season?

pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Hornets final score: Cade Cunningham powers second-half surge in blowout win
pistons.body:
CHARLOTTE, NC - NOVEMBER 2: Cade Cunningham #2 of the Detroit Pistons looks on during the game against the Charlotte Hornets on November 2, 2026 at Spectrum Center in Charlotte, North Carolina. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Kent Smith/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

The Detroit Pistons played great basketball throughout the night, but the Charlotte Hornets just kept hanging around. The Pistons were shooting better than 60% from the floor and 50% from three, and yet a Dennis Schroder layup made it a two-possession game with just under five minutes left in the second quarter. Then Cade Cunningham took over, then the Detroit Pistons took over, and suddenly a squeaker turned into a 124-91 Detroit win.

In that decisive 45-16 run, Cade Cunningham scored 14 points, and he did it in under three and a half minutes of game time. One of the league’s best players finally had his first superstar quarter of the season, scoring 17 points and notching three assists in total in that decisive third frame. He finished the night with 33 points, seven assists, and five steals. In those magical few minutes, he was everywhere in his bag. Patient mid-range pull-ups, slicing through the D for layups, catch-and-shoot threes. He went to the bench with 1:17 left in the third quarter, and you were left thinking he might hit 50 in the fourth. But he never needed to come back in the game again.

He saw the game was getting too close, and he decided to do something about it. He put the team on his back and said, “We’re playing too well to not blow these guys out.”

But the true blowout wouldn’t have happened without all the other contributions up and down the lineup. The Pistons really have something on offense this season, and while the range of ball handlers and actions can lead to some self-inflicted wounds, it is designed to open up this offense and let it breathe. And, boy, did they take a big gulping breath versus the Hornets.

The Pistons shot 57% from the floor and 48% from deep, and that was dragged down a bit as a consequence of some extended garbage time. The Pistons also kept their defense in top form. They forced 25 Charlotte turnovers, and that led to 27 fast-break points.

Detroit was led by Cade, but Duncan Robinson continues to be lights out this season. He shot 6-of-9 from deep on his way to 24 points. His stroke was immediate and effortless. He’s truly in the zone. Some of that shooting magic might be rubbing off on Kevin Huerter. The one-time bucket has struggled from deep for a few seasons now, including his short stint after a mid-season trade to Detroit last season. But he hit three threes tonight and is now shooting 38% from deep for the season. Even Ron Holland canned three threes tonight. Not to be overlooked is Ausar Thompson’s expanded role in the offense.

It’s not always perfect, but Thompson is getting more comfortable making decisions with the ball in his hands, and he’s understanding how to make defense pay by using his strength and burst to get something close to the basket. Thompson was 5-of-7 from the floor for 14 points, and he added six rebounds and four assists.

The Pistons had plenty of lopsided runs last season in their sprint to 60 wins. But those were driven by a defense that would suffocate you and an offense that could do just enough. Last year, the Pistons could go on a 27-2 run over the course of 17 minutes of game action. Tonight, they went on the same run in just over eight minutes.

Detroit’s defense remains the best in the league. Its offense is starting to catch up. That’s bad news for everyone else in the NBA.

It’s already time for a rematch, huh? The Detroit Pistons face the Charlotte Hornets for the second time this season. In the first matchup, the Pistons prevailed 97-89 behind a Cade Cunningham and Daniss Jenkins one-two punch at point guard. Cunningham had 30 points and seven assists, and Jenkins scored 14 points off the bench. They also got great contributions from Paul Reed (16 efficient points) and an all-around masterclass from Ausar Thompson, who tallied seven points, nine rebounds, and eight assists. It featured a great 31-point performance from the blossoming Brandon Miller and one of the season’s earliest head-scratchers. Naz Reid had seven points and six rebounds at halftime, but Hornets coach Charles Lee benched Reid for the entire second half for not meeting the “standards” of the team. Nothing stood out as egregious, and folks chalked it up to mixing up some defensive assignments and a lack of hustle. It was a surprising but short-lived kerfuffle (Reid’s been back in the lineup ever since). But I wouldn’t be surprised if the Hornets power forward is looking to make a statement against Detroit so as to truly put the situation to rest.

The Hornets are struggling to find their offense after moving on from LaMelo Ball and getting a bum hand via injuries — Kon Knueppel and Grant Williams are both going to miss the game tonight. That means the league’s least potent (statistically) offense is going to go up against the league’s most miserly defense (statistically). pistons.headline: Pistons vs Nets final score: Detroit takes care of business in first NBA Cup game
pistons.body:
BROOKLYN, NY - OCTOBER 30: Ronald Holland II #5 of the Detroit Pistons dunks the ball during the game against the Brooklyn Nets during the 2026 Emirates NBA Cup on October 30, 2026 at Barclays Center in Brooklyn, New York. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Nathaniel S. Butler/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

The Detroit Pistons start the NBA Cup off with a bang. Detroit thumped the Brooklyn Nets 110-94. A plus-16 point differential is a solid start on their quest to win their first NBA Cup in franchise history.

Detroit’s defense got off to an uncharacteristic start. They got mixed up on several pick-and-roll possessions, but that didn’t last long. They figured out the Nets’ speedy guards. Nolan Traoré turns on the turbos when turning the corners. Detroit adjusted to his speed and Julius Randle’s bully ball style of play.

For the second straight game, Detroit held their opponents to a seemingly never-ending scoring drought. The Pistons hard-hedged, blitzed, and switched PnRs depending on their personnel on the floor. It’s a luxury to have so many versatile defenders.

The John Collins at the five lineups always present a different look. It’s a lot of speed out there when Detroit goes small. The lineups with Paul Reed aren’t technically small ball, but J.B. Bickerstaff can employ him so many different ways. Reed is not too much of a drop big, but he pressures guards coming off screens in every other way.

When Detroit did go small, Duncan Robinson and Kevin Huerter got their hands dirty helping the team gang rebound. It didn’t register in the box score every time, but the fight was there. Huerter was scrappy and hit a pair of first-half triples. His explosion from trey is coming. I will remain patient and will take all the other little things he’s doing.

Robinson is off to a career-best start. The 3s were hit or miss, but he thrived in transition and baited Brooklyn into several turnovers. Robinson is such an educated cutter. Teams press up on him, sticking to him like gum under the desk, but he has no issue using their momentum against them, beelining to the rim.

Robinson and Ausar connected on some backdoor cuts. Their synergy is so evident. They burned another defense with their DHO link-up.

We got aggressive Ausar tonight. Right from the opening tap, he searched for his shot and was content to put his head down to get to the rim.

Ausar Thompson that was beautiful pic.twitter.com/1Z3C6BE6Nd
— mm (@muhtxm) October 31, 2026

We got a middy pull-up in the second! Ausar was feeling it and took another jumper the following possession. Make or miss, that is the mentality that can change this team’s outlook.

Ausar’s all-around play was terrific. We’re watching a legit point forward in the making game by game. Ausar had six assists tonight. This one was gorgeous.

Ausar with the behind the back dish 👀 pic.twitter.com/rhArT0m6sk
— Detroit Pistons (@DetroitPistons) October 31, 2026

Ausar’s 9-to-5 defensive intensity clone, Ron Holland, had himself a ball game. He had a turnover and ill-advised fouls early on, but Holland turned it up a notch in the 3rd quarter.

The third-year wing was EVERYWHERE. His hound-em defense showed up, but Holland buried two 3-pointers during his energy blitz. He finished with 18 points, going 6-for-10 from the field, along with four steals.

It was another day in the office for Deuce. He might be the first player to get a foul called in their favor in real time. He did the classic Kobe/DWade up fake, then shoot while the defender is off their feet. It did not seem like the referee was going to reward Cade’s craftiness until he walked over there with wide-spread arms demanding an explanation. Nice to see Cade getting that superstar whistle these days. He dropped 20/5/4.

Brooklyn remains winless (0-5). Traoré is a blur, and Mikel Brown Jr. seems to process PnR coverages like a point guard who’s been around the block. That dude has promise. High process and deep-range shooting is always a dub in my book. Brooklyn fans won’t enjoy watching Randle go one-on-one with 10 eyes staring at him, waiting for his drive, but hey, it’s not all bad elsewhere. Focus on the young guards.

Ebuka Okorie probably gets more run in a typical blowout. Detroit aimed to run up the score for the cup point differential, so that might explain why Bickerstaff went with his proven horses until it was less than three minutes in the contest.

Detroit’s 2025 second-round pick Chaz Lanier got in on the action. He knocked down two deep balls with his quick trigger release. This was a monster performance from Detroit after their defense got back on a string. Brooklyn isn’t the 1996 Bulls but has competed in most of their games so far. Not tonight.

Detroit looks to beat up on the Charlotte Hornets again to kick off their November schedule on Monday. Maybe they get Charlotte so discombobulated that Charles Lee has to bench another starter.

(Daniss had another end-of-quarter buzzer-beater. Add this one to the highlight reel)

He's good at that. https://t.co/sYGm01ubBO pic.twitter.com/b6SJHj4SCu
— Detroit Pistons (@DetroitPistons) October 31, 2026

pistons.headline: The Pindown: The Pistons are a Good Team… Again
pistons.body:
While Robbie is out celebrating, Blake returns to discuss the impressive wins the Pistons have earned over the past week. lions.headline: Lions, Dolphins Week 9 injury designations: Lions rule out 5 starters
lions.body:
Detroit Lions center Cade Mays (64) warms up ahead of the game between Detroit Lions and Minnesota Vikings at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The Detroit Lions (5-2) and Miami Dolphins (1-6) have declared their Week 9 injury designations, and the Lions will be missing multiple starters, including one on offense, three on defense, and one not yet cleared from his injury list—all of which we knew ahead of time, based on coach Dan Campbell’s comments throughout the week.

Let’s look at Friday’s practice report and get you up to date on what we know.

Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded.

Ruled OUT

C Cade Mays (ankle) — Preparing for Juice Scruggs to start

EDGE DJ Wonnum (concussion)

LB Jack Campbell (neck)

CB D.J. Reed (hip)

S Kerby Joseph (knee, PUP) — Days remaining in injury evaluation clock: 11

Mays is dealing with a low ankle sprain, which typically keeps players out at least a week, and potentially as long as a month, so him being ruled out of this game was expected. How quickly he recovers is still to be determined, but the Lions have been highly fortunate to have Juice Scruggs stepping into the starting center role, and they’ve been planning on him starting since the beginning of this week.

Wonnum is still working through the NFL’s concussion protocols and won’t be able to return in time for this game. With head injury recovery times varying by individual, it’s unclear how long he will need before he is cleared. Second-round rookie Derrick Moore is expected to increase his role in Wonnum’s absence, and Campbell is seeing improvement:

“It was unfortunate we lost Wonnum, but yet, now (Moore) gets more reps. And the reps that he got are valuable, man. There’s no way to duplicate real in time game reps against good opponents and you see growth, you see growth. I saw growth in practice yesterday. So, the more he plays, the better he’s going to get. And we love where he’s going right now.”

Jack Campbell continues to improve, per Dan Campbell, but he should be considered out indefinitely until otherwise clarified.

“Jack continues to improve, which is all great news,” Dan Campbell said on Friday.

Reed said he felt good in the locker room following the game, but he was not cleared to practice this week and will miss this game. Campbell noted that he’s very confident with the team’s depth:

“(Ennis) Rakestraw is getting better. Rock (Ya-Sin) looks healthy and is playing good football. (Roger) McCreary, too. So, I just feel like these guys are starting to play pretty good football for us. And (Khalil) Dorsey, man, Dorsey’s contributing in a big way. So, I like where we’re at and it’s really a pretty depthwise, it’s a pretty strong room. So yeah, I don’t like the though of not having Reed, but at the same time, I’m encouraged. I’m encouraged. I think we’ll be OK here.”

Joseph is looking “better than anticipated,” according to safeties coach Jim O’Neil, but Campbell made it clear earlier in the week that the plan was to keep him out for another game, then continue to ramp up his participation levels next week, as he nears a return.

“It’s been great. Two weeks ago, it was classroom work, where we were really locked in. Then it was walkthrough and individual. Yesterday was his first team practice and he looked a lot better than what I anticipated him looking (like). So it was very encouraging. So now he’s gotta stack multiple days. He’s got to stack them, so today will be a big day for him, but he looked awesome yesterday at practice,” O’Neill said on Friday.

Questionable

RB Sione Vaki (ankle) — added to the injury report on Friday

RB Jacob Saylors (neck)

WR Amon-Ra St. Brown (rib)

Vaki was unexpectedly absent from Friday’s practice and has been given a questionable designation heading into this weekend’s game. Beyond that, the extent of his injury is unknown, and we may have to wait until Saturday—to see if he travels with the team—or even game time on Sunday, to find out his availability.

Saylors has dealt with a neck injury for two weeks and couldn’t finish Week 7’s game against the Vikings because of it. Look for the Lions to be cautious in his return, but with Vaki also questionable, the Lions could end up with a depth issue at running back.

St. Brown was injured in Week 7 but told the media on Thursday that, “I’m a little banged up, but I’ll be alright,” and is anticipating playing against the Dolphins.

Not listed with an injury designation

LB Amen Ogbongbemiga (toe)

CB Rock Ya-Sin (cramps)

S Brian Branch (concussion)

Ogbongbemiga was estimated to have been a limited participant on Wednesday and a full participant after that, and with him not carrying an injury designation, he should be good to go, giving the Lions special teams work and linebacker depth.

Ya-Sin dealt with cramps earlier in the week but still practiced in full each day. He’s potentially in line to challenge for a starting role this week with Reed sidelined.

Branch is nearing the end of the NFL’s concussion protocol, and Campbell said he expects him to be cleared and ready to play on Sunday.

“I think (Brian Branch) BB’s going to be good here. We’ll get through today, and I think we’ll be OK.”

lions.headline: Lions safety Kerby Joseph looking ‘better than anticipated’
lions.body:
ALLEN PARK, MI - AUGUST 08: Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph (31) participates in pass coverage drills during the Detroit Lions Training Camp afternoon practice session on August 8, 2022 at the the Detroit Lions Training Facility in Allen Park, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph won’t play this week, as he continues to ramp up from a knee injury that cost him over a year of football activities. But as he continues to get more work in and get close to his return to the field, Joseph is starting to turn heads.

Last week, the Lions started his 21-day evaluation clock, getting him worked into walkthrough practices while getting additional reps with teammates after practice. This week, he got his first taste of team action, and he was already doing things Lions safeties coach Jim O’Neill wasn’t expecting.

“It’s been great. Two weeks ago, it was classroom work, where we were really locked in. Then it was walkthrough and individual. Yesterday was his first team practice, and he looked a lot better than what I anticipated him looking (like),” O’Neil said. “So it was very encouraging. So now he’s gotta stack multiple days. He’s got to stack them, so today will be a big day for him, but he looked awesome yesterday at practice.”

O’Neil credited a lot of people in Joseph’s recovery. There’s the medical staff that has outlined and executed a recovery plan for the safety. There are players like Dominic Lovett and Jackson Meeks, who have stayed after practice to help get Joseph caught up on the reps he’s missed in practice during his ramp-up. But more than anyone, O’Neil credits Joseph’s perseverance through the difficult last couple of years.

“He’s worked his ass off. He has. He’s gone through a mental battle, he’s gone through a physical battle, and he’s in a great place right now,” O’Neil said. “And I’m excited for him, and I know how hard he’s working. I know how hard it must be to be at the top of your game and then have it taken away from you. He’s grinded to get back to the level that he’s used to playing at and at his standard.”

The next step for Joseph is simple: stack days. It’s not just about how his knee responds to a heavier load, but how Joseph himself can continue to play and grow. As O’Neil is quick to point out, Joseph hasn’t really played at a Pro Bowl level in nearly two years, as he was battling through this knee injury even when he was playing in 2025.

But if the Lions can get the 2024 Kerby Joseph back—along with Brian Branch’s continued progress now that he’s back from his 2025 Achilles injury—then Detroit’s back-end could look a lot different and better soon.

“As we get guys back, guys like with Kerby’s skillset or (Thomas) Harper’s skillset, that just opens up the door to do more stuff with Branch,” O’Neil said. “He can go down, he can do dime roles, he can play nickel roles. You can use him more of a chess piece as we get some guys back in the defense and in that secondary.”

lions.headline: Has the Detroit Lions defense turned a corner?
lions.body:
What a difference a month can make. After a historically bad start to the season, Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard has helped the defense find their sea legs over the course of the last four weeks. With that said, there is still plenty to improve upon for a unit that has even more to play for with the loss of All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell during their Week 8 win over the Minnesota Vikings.

There were some around the fan base and media who were ready to move on from Sheppard if things didn’t improve—especially after the loss to the Carolina Panthers where they appeared to be out-schemed from the jump. After some tough conversations as well as some schematic and personnel tweaks, the Lions’ defense is beginning to settle in dating back to their Week 5 whooping of the Arizona Cardinals.

That brings us to today’s Question of the Day:

Do you believe the Lions’ defense has turned a corner?

My answer: Despite a three-game sample size not being the largest to go off of, I do belive this unit has begun to figure things out. It still isn’t perfect, and there are still too many missed assignments for my liking, but you can do a lot with the way the Lions’ front is playing. Their star players up front, like defensive end Aidan Hutchinson and defensive tackle Alim McNeill, are making their presence felt nearly every time the ball is snapped.

Beyond those two, other members of the defensive line like rookie Skyler Gill-Howard and second year defensive tackle Tyleik Williams are playing some really good football. And while there are still things to clean up in the secondary, cornerback D.J. Reed’s play has really leveled out, star defensive back Brian Branch is back in the mix, and the team opened up All-Pro safety Kerby Joseph’s 21-day window last week.

If they can continue to defend the run well and cut down on the blown coverage moments that have plagued them through seven games, I think that will be enough to make them a contender down the stretch. Continue to improve so that you are playing your best, and most sound football in December and into January. When you have an offense like Detroit does, that’s all you really need.

The following week, Branch had another helmet-to-helmet collision, this time with teammate DJ Wonnum. The collision knocked both Wonnum and Branch out of the game with a concussion.

Violent collisions with his helmet are nothing new with Branch. He’s been fined six times for impermissible use of his helmet, twice for hit on a defenseless receiver, and he was ejected from a game after a particularly violent head-to-head collision vs. the Packers in 2024.

Despite the two notable collisions through two games, Lions safeties coach Jim O’Neil offered an impassioned defense of Branch’s play.

“We coach eyes-up tackle, but we also coach—we’re going to play the game violently,” O’Neil said. “That’s the way the game was meant to play. That’s one of the reasons BB is who he is. I mean, he’s got an old-school mentality. He’s explosive. He’s going to play the game violently. We talk about defending every blade of grass, whether it’s on the sideline—you’re not going to tiptoe the sideline on us. If a running back’s on his way down, we’re going to beat him to the ground and hit him.

“I thought BB did a great job on that play. He lowered his target. Obviously, when the receiver drops, as well, sometimes it’s head-to-head. We’ll continue to coach eyes-up tackle, but I love the way Brian Branch plays, and we’re not going to do anything to change that. We’re going to continue to try to help him with his technique, but we’re not going to change his mentality at all.”

Earlier in the week, coach Dan Campbell made a similar argument about Branch.

“Once he’s going, he’s going for his target and then that target drops. And so, that ends up where it goes,” Campbell said. “You can certainly say go lower, but now you have got to be careful. You start going real low, then you start taking out knees and stuff, and you don’t want any of that. So, just keep your eyes up, see what you hit, try to drop it just a little bit.”

Branch is progressing through concussion protocol, and barring any setback, the Lions expect him to play this week vs. the Miami Dolphins. That’s good news for Detroit, because O’Neil compared Branch’s versatility to having three extra players on defense.

“I think as we get into the third, fourth, fifth game here, he’s going to catch his groove,” O’Neil said. “He’s such a unique piece, because he can play like a linebacker, he can play like a corner, he can play like a safety. It’s like having three extra guys up on game day, because of what he can do for the defense.”

lions.headline: Lions vs. Dolphins: 3 key matchups
lions.body:
The Detroit Lions (5-2) take their talents to South Beach to take on the Miami Dolphins (1-6). Fresh off a three-game win streak, including two in a row against the Green Bay Packers and Minnesota Vikings, the Lions have reestablished themselves as true NFC North contenders.

Despite the back-to-back-to-back victories, the Lions still find themselves currently in third place in the division. This week, the Chicago Bears take on the rising Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and the Minnesota Vikings host Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills on “Monday Night Football.” If the Lions take care of their business, there is a realistic opportunity that Dan Campbell’s team will sit alone at the top of the standings.

From just about every performance and talent metric, the Lions should have the edge in this matchup. But digging deeper, the Dolphins are rebuilding in a way that should remind Lions fans of the Dan Campbell led 2021 team.

In what could typically be labeled a “trap game,” often the NFL rears its powerful element of parity into the equation. To avoid that, the key matchups will come down to not necessarily the talent on the field, the grit of the players to determine the ultimate outcome.

Let’s dive in to the three key matchups centered on the intangible traits that will make or break Sunday’s matchup in south Florida.

Gritty rookies in key roles

Breaking the normal structure of the article here as this first key matchup really is not a direct positional or players matchup, but the comparative play of the key rookies on each team. While many readers here at Pride of Detroit are familiar the Grit Index, for newer readers, it is the NFL Draft metric that Erik Schlitt and I have created to grade prospects on their intangible qualities.

In the 2026 NFL Draft, seven teams drafted players in the elite tier of the Grit Index with a score of 9+. The Detroit Lions and Miami Dolphins were two of those teams.

There were 30 players with a 9+ score on this year’s GRIT Index (top ~7.5%)

Only 2 teams drafted 3 or more players within this Elite tier:

— Chicago (4 – Thieneman, Roush, Jones, Elliott)
— Detroit (3 – Miller, Abney, Gill-Howard)

(2 – BAL, IND, LV, MIA, PIT)
— Between The Numbers – Anthony (@BtwnTheNumbers) April 26, 2026

For the Lions, it was Blake Miller, Keith Abney, and Skyler Gill-Howard. For the Dolphins, it was Jacob Rodriguez and Michael Taaffe.

You could call it coincidence, but I am not surprised that each of these five rookies have become key contributors for their respective teams. In fact, Rodriguez and Taaffe are first and second, respectively, in snaps played on the entire Dolphins roster. Similarly, Miller, Abney, and Gill-Howard lead the Lions 2026 rookie draft class in snap counts on the season.

They key here with all five of these players is which one will either rise to the occasion, or which one will be a potential liability? Rookies go through growing pains and not all progress is linear. Will Taaffe rise to the occasion against the Lions elite offensive weapons? Will Rodriguez command and communicate the defense to his teammates as the green dot linebacker against the creatively-detailed Lions offense run by offensive coordinator Drew Petzing and Jared Goff?

Will the Lions rookies take their strong starts to the next level, or will it be a game filled with growing pains coming off a three-game win streak?

The play of these rookies will go a long way in determining the outcome of the game.

The Lions’ linebacker room

This is a big week. At this point, we’re all aware of and have been in the emotional waiting room following the updates and progression after Jack Campbell’s traumatic neck injury against the Vikings. The impact, though, is most significantly felt by those players closest to him.

The key matchup is not how fellow linebackers Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Trevor Nowaske fill in Jack Campbell’s shoes, no player will be able to do that for this team. And I don’t suspect they are trying to.

The key is how Barnes, Rodriguez, and Nowaske can play as the best version of themselves and as a unit while battling this adversity on and off the field.

Derrick Barnes wept in the locker room. Malcolm Rodriguez spent the first night "hugging my family." Even Alex Anzalone was hurting in Tampa Bay.

But the season continues, and "he doesn’t want us to feel sorry for him."

"Prepare and play like 46." https://t.co/Fv9KTOtsMo
— Will Burchfield (@burchie_kid) November 5, 2026

In my view, having Kelvin Sheppard as defensive coordinator, former linebacker coach, and former linebacker himself, he is in a unique position to lead these players through this storm. Sheppard has expressed nothing but confidence in the group.

“I raised these other guys that are about to play. Malcolm Rodriguez and Derrick Barnes, those are my little brothers and they know the standard. They both have worn the green dot before. So, this isn’t like a first-time ordeal for either one of them, because that load might get shared. We’re still working through that, but I’m confident in either one of them.”

I don’t expect this group to be perfect as each player adapts to their adjusted roles. But I do expect each to play with passion and grit. I expect them to prepare and play like 46.

Zach Sieler vs. Lions interior offensive line

Lastly, turning to the leader of the Dolphins, captain Zach Sieler is not only the fins most disruptive player on defense, he is the heart and soul of the team.

🎥 Jeff Hafley on Zach Sieler's leadership: "It's valuable to me, it's valuable to the young players… he's one of the best people ever. There's not a much better person out there than Zach Sieler. He does everything the right way." (@MiamiDolphins) #PhinsUp pic.twitter.com/gal8hkUSCF
— FinsXtra (@FinsXtra) October 5, 2026

Dan Campbell has emphasized Sieler’s impact.

“Defensively, Sieler’s really the anchor in there. You know, he’s played good football for a really long time, man. Smart, crafty, powerful, can get an edge in the pass game.”

Relentless in both the run and pass game, Sieler will present a challenge to the youth of the Lions interior offensive line. With starting center Cade Mays not practicing and a wave of injuries on defense, the Lions can control the game if Christian Mahogany, Juice Scruggs, and Tate Ratledge can continue to win the line of scrimmage along the interior.

In a game where, On Paper, the Lions have a distinct advantage, players like Sieler can lead the charge in a spoiler’s effort.

Three key matchups. Three opportunities for grit to win the day.

lions.headline: Lions vs. Dolphins 5 Qs preview: Is Miami mirroring Detroit’s 2021 culture rebuild?
lions.body:
Dan Campbell guides the Lions through workouts during a spring minicamp. 2022-06-10 Dan Campbell | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The Detroit Lions head to South Beach for a Week 9 interconference matchup against a young, rebuilding Miami Dolphins team.

We had the pleasure of connecting with Kevin Nogle, the Managing Editor of Phinsider to give us some insight into this Miami team ahead of Sunday’s kickoff. We learned about the local sentiment surrounding head coach Jeff Hafley’s foundational reset, how offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik is tailoring the offense to quarterback Malik Willis, and how Ollie Gordon is handling the backfield workload in De’Von Achane’s absence—plus what Miami needs to do to keep pace with Detroit’s offense.

1. Miami arguably made more changes to their organization than any other team in the NFL this offseason. New head coach, new quarterback, the changing out of long-tenured skill position players—it was a massive overhaul in South Beach.

Although the Dolphins are off to a 1-6 start, how much of that was expected from a team that underwent so many changes this offseason? It’s early, but do you get the sense that new head coach Jeff Hafley is the right guy for this rebuild?

This year is about setting up the franchise for the future, and while losses are never fun, the struggles were expected. This is the league’s youngest team, and they are facing a steep learning curve. Miami has 14 rookies on the roster, plus another seven first-year players. This is clearly a reset of the team’s foundation, and there will be growing pains.

The Dolphins’ schedule has also been brutal this year. They started the year against the Las Vegas Raiders, San Francisco 49ers, Kansas City Chiefs, and Minnesota Vikings, not facing a team that had a loss until Week 5 against the Cincinnati Bengals, who were 2-2 coming into that game. Through Week 8, Miami has faced the league’s toughest schedule, with a combined opponent winning percentage of .589. The schedule is not an excuse, but with such a young team, it is another variable to consider.

Obviously, things can change, but Hafley has instilled confidence in the fanbase so far. The Mike McDaniel era had some fun moments, but it quickly fell apart and the team never adjusted (and McDaniel still does not seem to have made adjustments as the Los Angeles Chargers struggle this year). I think Hafley’s focus on making the Dolphins physical, allowing the younger players to gain experience, and the team’s ability to make adjustments, learn from mistakes, and continue to fight even in losing situations indicate he is the right guy for this role. Lions fans saw Dan Campbell build a culture out of tough losses back in 2021; that is exactly the phase Hafley and the Dolphins are in right now.

2. From the outside looking in, Malik Willis was dropped into a tough situation given the pieces around him in the offense—and it looks like, predictably, the passing game has struggled so far. The Dolphins rank 26th in passing DVOA and EPA/pass.

How has Bobby Slowik tried to tailor this offense to Willis’ strengths? What’s working, what’s not working, and how much of that is related to a new quarterback in a new system versus the lack of talent personnel-wise?

I think we are starting to see Willis find some comfort in the offensive system, and he is starting to play better. Despite being a third-round pick in 2022, Willis has played in only 29 career games, starting just 13. He is a league veteran but really has the starting experience of a rookie. At times, he still seems bothered by the speed of the game, but the experience he is getting this year is already making a difference in his play.

I think one of the biggest issues we have seen from Willis is a desire to be a pocket passer. He stays in the pocket longer than he should, trying to find the perfect pass rather than taking something shorter or throwing the ball away to avoid a sack. The offensive line is not doing him any favors, but he has taken multiple sacks by running out of bounds instead of throwing the ball away. He seemed to want to avoid using his legs, but has opened up that part of his game in the last couple of weeks.

Slowik, like McDaniel before him, has an offensive system built on quarterback accuracy and timing. He uses bootlegs, run-pass options, and play-action passes to get Willis out of the pocket and seeing open receivers. They also seem to be using some half-field concepts, keeping Willis looking in one area and working from deep to shallow rather than having him search the entire field for receivers.

The youth on the roster – especially with wide receivers Caleb Douglas, Chris Bell, and Kevin Coleman Jr. – do not always create separation, and drops have also been an issue. When the primary target is not open on time, a young quarterback hesitates, and behind an evolving offensive line, hesitation leads to sacks. That all relates back to the discussion of Miami’s reset this year. The potential for talent is on Miami’s roster, but they still need to grow individually and together. The coaching staff is clearly working on the balance between youth and system – relying on a more basic system as the players learn.

3. Losing De’Von Achane in the first month of the season felt especially cruel for this offense that was already so limited on difference makers. The Dolphins rank 9th in EPA/rush (-0.03) but rank near the bottom of the league in rush success rate (26th) and rush DVOA (26th), suggesting that their run game is a boom-or-bust attack.

Is that a fair assessment of Ollie Gordon’s performance this year? The Dolphins also rank 26th in stuffed rate (22.8%) which is the percentage of runs that earn zero or negative yards. Are those stuffed runs more of an indictment of the offensive line or the coaching/play calling?

That seems like a fair assessment. Gordon has been a lot of fun to watch as he breaks out this year, but he is a power-back who works extremely well as a change-of-pace option behind Achane. When he finds space, he is able to break it for a big gain, but it really is boom or bust on each run.

Part of that is Gordon and his abilities. Part of that is the offensive line finding space to get him free. And part of that is opposing defenses planning to stop the run. Miami has had success this year, averaging 131 rushing yards per game, and they have topped 100 yards in five of seven games, including one game over 150 yards and another over 200 yards. They also have two games with 74 yards rushing each. Boom or bust.

The offensive line—especially last week with Kadyn Proctor out with a concussion—still has work to do to come together as a unit.

I think play calling is part of it, but not necessarily because the plays are wrong, but rather because the player is wrong. The rushing attack was built for Achane’s skill set, complemented by Gordon. Now, it is a Gordon-led unit and some of the designs are clearly meant for Achane’s speed over Gordon’s power. We have seen that evolve as Slowik has adjusted to Gordon, but there is an obvious difference between the two players and there will likely be a boom or bust aspect to the Dolphins’ ground game all season. The outside zone, stretch concepts were designed for Achane’s elite sideline-to-sideline track speed. Gordon is a one-cut, downhill runner. The Dolphins have pivoted to more gap and inside-zone looks to match Gordon’s style, but until defenses are forced to back out of the box, stops will linger.

4. Hafley brings his decades of experience coaching defense to Miami, and the numbers related to personnel deployment and coverage usage are pretty interesting through eight weeks. Miami lines up in base personnel 51.7% of snaps, second-most in the NFL, and they’re utilizing zone coverage 78.8% of the time (10th in the NFL).

How much of these numbers overlap with the talent available on the current roster? In other words, does it feel like Hafley’s trying to put his players in the best spots to succeed? Numbers suggest the run defense is bordering on being a top-10 unit, but the pass defense might be the worst in the league. Do those numbers tell the whole story?

Hafley definitely relies on base defense and he expects his front four to create pressure, rather than relying on the blitz—especially when compared to someone like Brian Flores, a former Dolphins head coach, and his blitz heavy defense. Hafley expects the pressure to come from the front four, allowing him to keep additional players back in coverage or focused on the run. It has been successful—at least as successful as can be expected with the younger players executing on the field.

The run defense has been strong for much of the year. There have been mistakes, especially when an edge rusher bites on a play action, chasing the quarterback and failing to set the edge or runs right past the ball carrier, but overall, they are doing well against the run. Of course, I say all of that knowing full well Jahmyr Gibbs is second in the league in rushing and is averaging nearly five-yards-per-carry, so the pressure is on the defense to continue to find success this week.

Does the contrast between the pass defense and the run defense tell the entire story? Not necessarily. The heavy zone scheme with the younger defensive backs is designed to prevent explosive, 60+ yard plays. That is allowing for short and intermediate routes to pick apart defenses (especially when Miami struggles to cover tight ends. Good thing the Lions are not bringing a top-tier tight end into this game, right?!?). Add in that Miami has been playing from behind for much of the year, and the short, possession passing game has been highly effective.

I do think Hafley is keeping his defensive calls a little more basic than maybe we will see from him in the next few years, allowing the foundation to be set before he starts building off of it. The Dolphins have stressed that they expect to build for the future through the draft and grow the team from within. If they stick to that plan, I think you will see both the offense and defense evolve as the players grow and Miami moves from a roster dominated by rookies to one with veterans hitting their prime supported by key rookies each year.

5. The Dolphins opened as 7-point home underdogs over at FanDuel Sportsbook heading into this Week 9 matchup against the Lions. What’s one thing you want to see, what’s one thing you need to see, and one thing you’re sure you’ll see happen in this matchup between the Lions and Dolphins on Sunday afternoon?

I want to see the offense be aggressive and take shots downfield. The Lions are allowing 276 yards per game through the air, and they are banged up. Let Willis test them early, get Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell into the game, and use the play-action to create opportunities. The Dolphins need to come into this game feeling like they have to win in a shoot-out. If they are aggressive on offense, maybe they can catch the Lions a little flat-footed at the start.

I need to see the Dolphins continue to make adjustments week-to-week, correct mistakes from the last game, and grow as a unit. That will be true throughout this season. Continued growth week to week is important and seeing the team not make the same mistakes over and over will continue to keep Dolphins fans confident the team is headed in the right direction.

I am sure I will see the Dolphins compete in this game and play hard through the fourth quarter. They may not be biting kneecaps (I love Dan Campbell and miss him in Miami), but they should be physical and give it everything they have on every down. I am also sure I will see Campbell continue to be aggressive on third- and fourth-down. The Dolphins have allowed over 50 percent conversion for opposing offenses on third down this year. They have to expect the Lions to attack on third down, and then attack again on fourth down.

The Lions are coming into this game as the better team. They should leave Miami having proven they are the better team. But, if Miami executes well, they can at least stand toe-to-toe with Detroit throughout the game, take the punches, and fight through the final bell. Really, the Dolphins have the ability to be the 2021 Lions – growing with a first-year head coach, taking a bad season and turning it into the foundation for a brighter future. If Miami can follow the same pathway as the Lions, this would be a successful rebuild.

lions.headline: Detroit Lions vs. Miami Dolphins preview, prediction: On Paper
lions.body:
MIAMI, FL - OCTOBER 21: Matthew Stafford #9 of the Detroit Lions in action against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium on October 21, 2018 in Miami, Florida. (Photo by Mark Brown/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Lions are beat up after a physical and emotional win over the Minnesota Vikings. And while they must travel to play a 1-6 Miami Dolphins team, they can’t afford to underestimate them. The NFC North is too competitive for a trap game, and the Dolphins are a little scrappier than they appear.

But is there a real chance of an upset in Miami, or are the Lions clearly the better team? Let’s examine it in our Lions vs. Dolphins preview and prediction. It’s time for On Paper.

Lions pass offense (8th in DVOA) vs. Dolphins pass defense (29th)

The Lions’ passing offense remains one of their most reliable units on the team. While last week’s performance against the Vikings wasn’t explosive, it was certainly a lot better than most teams manage against Minnesota’s defense. While the DVOA ranking remains outside the top five, I still believe Detroit’s passing attack should be in that top tier.

For the season, they rank:

Fourth in passer rating (110.0)

Seventh in yards per attempt (7.9)

Third in dropback EPA (0.264)

First in EPA/pass (+0.21)

Fourth in dropback success rate (51.4%)

Detroit is humming in all facets of their passing attack. In pass protection, the Lions allow the fifth-lowest pressure percentage (30.1%), rank seventh in pass-block win rate (54%), and rank third in PFF team pass-blocking grade (75.1).

The Dolphins may have a worse pass defense than the Lions. Five out of the seven quarterbacks who have faced Miami have finished with a passer rating of 119.8 or higher. Granted, they’ve played some really good quarterbacks in Brock Purdy, Patrick Mahomes, Joe Burrow, and Drake Maye. Still, those quarterbacks have outperformed their year-long efficiency against Miami, and the DVOA ranking—which adjusts to opponents’ strength—proves this is a bad pass defense.

Overall, they rank:

32nd in passer rating allowed (119.5)

32nd in yards per attempt (8.3)

32nd in dropback EPA (0.288)

32nd in dropback success rate (53.7%)

This is the result of having an extremely young and inexperienced back seven.

Though there is some recent hope for Miami’s pass rush. As Erik Schlitt pointed out in his Honolulu Blueprint, while the season-long stats don’t look great for the Dolphins’ ability to get to the passer (35.6% pressure rate, 18th; 4.2% sack rate, 28th), they’ve started to put things together. All nine of their sacks have come in the last four games, and they’ve posted a pressure rate of 39.5% or higher in three out of four of those games (league average is around 36%).

Over those last four games, the Dolphins’ pass defense has been better, but certainly not good. From Weeks 4-8, Miami ranks 27th in dropback EPA (0.180) and 29th in success rate (50.7%).

Player to watch: Sam LaPorta. It’s been a quiet few weeks for the Lions tight end, but Miami is allowing the sixth-highest yardage to tight ends (483 yards) and tied for the fourth-most touchdowns (six).

Advantage: Lions +3. This is a top-five unit vs. a bottom-five unit. The only reason I’m not giving it a higher advantage is that some things are trending Miami’s way, and weather could also play a factor, with some slight chance of rain.

Lions run offense (4th) vs. Dolphins run defense (26th)

The Lions’ rushing attack still has frustrating bouts of inconsistency, but last week’s performance against the Vikings felt like a revelation. Whether Detroit’s sidecar formation was a Vikings-specific answer or the cracking of the code for the entire season, we’ll see. But it shows one thing for certain: Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing is capable of finding some answers.

For the season, the Lions rushing attack now ranks:

Ninth in yards per carry (4.6)

13th in rush EPA (-0.083)

Third in success rate (47.0%)

But I must continue to repeat myself that the negative plays are a big problem. The Lions’ 19.3% stuffed rate is sixth in the NFL. Those figures are down from last week (20.9%, third-highest), but it still remains an issue to track. Detroit’s power success rank also improved after last week, but they still rank just 24th, converting on just 59% of short-yardage situations.

Still, it’s worth pointing out how both the offensive line and the running backs are doing their parts. Detroit’s line ranks third in adjusted line yards, eighth in run block win rate, and fourth in PFF run blocking grade. Meanwhile, Detroit’s backfield ranks sixth in rushing yards over expected per rush (+0.5), sixth in yards after contact per rush (3.38), and Jahmyr Gibbs ranks fourth in missed tackle forced rate (31.9%).

This chart doesn’t exactly vibe with the Dolphins’ bottom-10 DVOA ranking. They’re not giving up a ton of yards nor a ton of yards per carry. So what gives? Let’s look deeper.

Eighth in yards per carry allowed (3.8)

22nd in rush EPA (-0.078)

30th in rush success rate (43.9%)

In short, it appears the Dolphins don’t give up a ton of big, explosive plays, but they essentially give up exactly what the offense needs. That’s backed by data. Miami has only given up 21 rushes of 10+ yards (t-14th), and just three rushes of 20+ yards (t-sixth fewest).

The good news is the Dolphins are weak where the Lions’ run offense struggles. They’ve produced just a 14.9% stuffed rate (23rd), and they rank 21st in power success rate, allowing conversions on 68% of short-yardage situations.

Player to watch: Jacob Rodriguez. The Dolphins rookie linebacker has been a fun player to watch thus far. Rodriguez has been credited with 30 “stops” per PFF (plays that are a failure for offense), which is second most among ALL NFL linebackers, not just rookies. Seventeen of those have come in the run, t-eighth most.

Advantage: Lions +1.5. I’m not sure I’d expect a huge game from Gibbs and company, given that Miami has not allowed over 150 rushing yards in a game. But Detroit should be fairly efficient on the ground.

Dolphins pass offense (26th) vs. Lions pass defense (24th)

It hasn’t been a great start to the year for Malik Willis in his new home, but it’s hard to blame him given the supporting cast. He’s got an extremely young receiving corps, a new offensive system, and an imbalanced offensive line. As a result, the Dolphins rank:

26th in passer rating (79.7)

20th in yards per attempt (6.9)

23rd in dropback EPA (0.014)

20th in dropback success rate (43.8%)

The Dolphins aren’t a complete disaster, but they’re clearly below average.

That said, there are some very interesting advanced statistics surrounding Willis. For one, he’s not afraid to chuck it deep. He currently owns the third-highest average depth of target (9.2), and his deep ball percentage of 16.4% ranks first in the NFL (yes, above Jordan Love, too). But he also ranks third in time to throw (3.05), suggesting he likely holds onto the ball too long—especially when you consider the Dolphins have the second-highest sack rate (10.3%).

The offensive line is a mixed bag. Though they’ve allowed the second-highest pressure rate (43.2%), they rank 20th in pass block win rate and 31st in PFF pass blocking grade. The issue is that the left side of their offensive line is good-to-great (LT Patrick Paul is 14th in pass blocking grade, rookie LG Kadyn Proctor is improving) and the right side is a disaster (RT Austin Jackson is dead last in pass blocking grade, RG Jonah Savaiinaea is 63rd out of 76).

And as mentioned before, the receiving corps is ridiculously young: Malik Washington is 25; Caleb Douglas is 23, and Chris Bell is 22. Young doesn’t mean bad, but it’ll take them some time to get adjusted to the NFL.

Is the Lions’ pass defense actually getting better? It’s hard for me to tell. The raw numbers are improving, but as the chart above shows, they’ve also played some pretty bad passing offenses in the last few weeks. I’m not yet convinced.

Overall, the Lions rank:

26th in passer rating allowed (101.0)

18th in yards per attempt (7.3)

29th in dropback EPA (0.218)

28th in success rate (50.0%)

I think it’s also worth noting that the Lions’ pass rush has fallen off a bit as of late. After three weeks, the Lions ranked 10th in pressure rate (39.0%) and second in time to pressure (2.46). The Lions now rank just 17th in pressure rate (35.8%) and 20th in time to pressure (2.68). And this week, they’re almost certainly without DJ Wonnum, who was fourth on the team in pressures (14). That said, the Lions still do rank third in pass rush win rate, third in PFF pass rush grade, and seventh in sack rate. I just worry it’s trending in the wrong direction.

Then, of course, there are the injuries to account for. While it looks like Brian Branch is on track to play, the Lions don’t have MIKE linebacker Jack Campbell, and top cornerback D.J. Reed is trending toward missing this game. Detroit’s back seven has already struggled immensely in coverage, and now they’ll be tested further.

Player to watch: Malik Washington. Washington leads the Dolphins in catches (31) and yards (329), and the Dolphins like to use him all over the field—as a screen weapon or downfield. His 4.47 speed is a weapon.

Advantage: Draw. I’m not particularly impressed with either unit. I think it’s certainly possible Willis hits on a few big downfield plays, and I think it’s also very possible Detroit is able to disrupt and sack Willis 4-6 times this game. In the end, I think it’ll all even out.

Dolphins run offense (26th) vs. Lions run defense (23rd)

This is another weird statistical oddity for Miami. By the charts, it looks like they actually have a good thing going with their run game, including a breakout season from Ollie Gordon (408 yards, 4.5 YPC, 4 TDs) and some quarterback rushing potential from Malik Willis (225 yards, 3 TDs). Yet, the advanced statistics aren’t as impressive. They rank:

11th in yards per carry (4.4)

21st in rush EPA (-0.128)

24th in success rate (36.0%)

It turns out this rushing attack is very boom or bust—like a less-efficient version of Detroit’s running game. They have produced t-sixth-most rushes of 10+ yards (26), but also a 19.1% stuff rate—seventh-highest.

The problem appears to be that the offensive line isn’t carrying their end of the bargain. They rank 26th in run block win rate, 27th in PFF run blocking grade, and 27th in adjusted line yards.

But credit to Gordon for doing everything he can to get the most out of his situation.

I don’t know, man. The Lions are just too inconsistent in the run game this year. They’ve been better lately, but it seems like they’re still susceptible to explosive plays. Overall, the Lions rank:

16th in yards per carry allowed (4.1)

17th in rush EPA (-0.096)

11th in success rate (37.2%)

So that pretty much matches my eye test. They’re decent down-to-down, but they give up too many explosives. Though they’ve only allowed 21 rushes of 10+ yards (t-14th fewest), they’ve allowed six of 20+ yards (t-ninth most).

And with the loss of Jack Campbell, it’s hard to know how this unit will respond. Detroit has an experienced linebacking corps in Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Trevor Nowaske, but none provide the instincts and consistency of Campbell.

Player to watch: Tyleik Williams. I pointed it out in my Dolphins vs. Patriots thoughts, but Miami really struggled against New England’s nose tackle last week, and Williams remains an impossible guy to move.

Advantage: Dolphins +1. I’m giving Miami a slight advantage here for a couple of reasons. First, I am concerned about the loss of Jack Campbell, and it may take a couple of weeks for Detroit to find a plan that works without him. Second, I do think Willis provides a legitimate rushing threat, and Detroit has lost contain far too often this year. Third, I just think Miami is better than their stats suggest, and the Lions may be a tad worse. It shouldn’t be a dominant day for Miami—and if Detroit can get out to a big lead, they can erase this advantage completely—but I still think Miami has the slight edge here.

Last week’s prediction:

On Paper drops to 5-2 overall and 3-4 against the spread, but I don’t feel all that bad for how my Lions vs. Vikings preview played out. The only area I made a clear mistake was underestimating the Lions’ run game, and for the first half of that game, I looked right. But Petzing made a lot of believers on Sunday, and I’m one of them.
