lions.headline: NFL predictions: 4 keys to a Lions victory over the Dolphins in Week 9
lions.body:
Oct 30, 2022; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) makes a pass against Miami Dolphins during the second half at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Junfu Han-USA TODAY Sports

The Detroit Lions (5-2) and Miami Dolphins (1-6) will face off in Week 9 in a battle between two teams at different stages in their regime builds. The Lions have their eyes firmly set on the postseason and are riding a three-game win streak, while the Dolphins are in the early stages of a rebuild and are performing much like the Lions did in 2021 and 2022—lots of grit, but struggling to find success.

“(Dolphins Head) Coach (Jeff) Hafley’s done a good job in his first year,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Wednesday. “A lot of similarities to—just reminds me a little of what we were when we came in. They’re young, they’re hungry, they’re active. They run, they hit, they hustle, they finish, try to play disciplined ball, and they’re playing that way.”

This week’s prediction preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook, who currently have the Lions listed at +1600 to win this year’s Super Bowl and are currently 7-point favorites in Week 9. Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Dolphins in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint.

Dolphins base scheme

For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 9 preview: Breaking down the Dolphins’ offensive and defensive schemes.

Prediction 1: Lions slow down pass rush with runs up the middle

Last Sunday, the Lions faced arguably the best defense in the NFL when they went head-to-head with the Vikings, and while the Dolphins are on the opposite end of the rankings spectrum, some of the strategies the Lions used against Minnesota will transfer over to this week’s game against Miami.

The Dolphins defense enters this game 29th in DVOA, 24th in points allowed (25.9), 24th in yards allowed per play (5.7 ypp), and are dead last in the NFL in three areas: EPA per play (+0.10), EPA per pass allowed (+0.26), and passing yards allowed per play (8.3).

However, this defense is showing growth in pressure rate. Looking at season totals, the Dolphins’ pressure numbers could be a bit deceiving: 31st in total pressures (77), 18th in pressure rate (35.6%), 30th in total sacks (9), and 28th in sack rate (4.2%). But when you look at the splits from their last four games, you can see the improvement:

at Vikings: 17 pressures, 39.5% pressure rate, 4 sacks, 9.3% sack rate

vs. Bengals: 11 pressures, 33.3% pressure rate, 0 sacks, 0% sack rate

at Jets: 15 pressures, 45.5% pressure rate, 2 sacks, 6.1% sack rate

vs. Patriots: 13 pressures, 48.1% pressure rate, 3 sacks, 11.1% sack rate

If we isolate the games against the Vikings, Jets, and Patriots, we see nearly 60% of the defensive pressures and 100% of the Dolphins sacks. When you look at how the Dolphins have generated pressures and sacks, most of those situations come from stunting their defensive linemen. Last week against the Patriots, the Dolphins sacked the quarterback once on an end-of-half situation, with the other two sacks coming off a stunt where an edge rusher loops behind the interior defensive lineman and twists inside. We also saw stunts get home against the Vikings in Week 4.

To counter the Dolphins’ stunts, offenses have been attacking the middle of the defensive line with their rushing attacks; teams are running inside 53% of the time, the sixth-highest rate in the NFL.

While the Lions have preferred to lean on their outside-zone rushing scheme, we saw last week against the Vikings that Detroit has a formula to get downhill on inside runs. Now, the Lions don’t necessarily need to deploy a full-house set (three players in the backfield) again, but it would certainly be effective against the Dolphins’ Wide-9 base 4-3 defense.

Prediction 2: Lions cross the zone to open the field for Goff

While all defenses are complex, at their core, the Dolphins split their defensive personnel almost evenly between a base 4-3 (three linebackers) front and a “Big Nickel” (three safeties) formation. Regardless of set, they spend about 80% of the time in zone coverage, with half of that time spent between single-high (Cover-1, -3) and two-high (Cover-2, -4, -6) safety sets. When they deploy man coverage, they run exclusively single-high Cover-1.

Depending on the safety formation, Lions quarterback Jared Goff will have to find the holes in the zone to exploit, but those gaps can widen if the Lions stretch the Dolphins laterally with their passing game. Based on the games I watched, the Dolphins’ defenders settle in their zones and tend to be slow to react to crossing routes in front of them. When offenses find success on crossers and stretch the zones across the field, that opens gaps down the deep seams, where speed receivers—hey, Jameson Williams—have found chunk plays.

If the Lions can slow the Dolphins’ pass rush with run up the middle, then stretch the secondary laterally, they’ll have an opportunity to chew up yards in a variety of ways.

Prediction 3: Lions match physicality; prevent explosive runs

When the Dolphins lost their dynamic running back De’Von Achane to an ACL injury in Week 3, many thought Miami’s rushing attack would struggle. However, second-year back Ollie Gordon has stepped into a starting role, and the Dolphins’ new downhill, physical rushing attack has proved to be an asset, even outproducing their early-season statistics, save last week vs. the Patriots. With quarterback Malik Willis adding another element to the run game through RPOs and scrambles, stopping the run will likely be the Lions’ top priority.

On paper, their raw numbers look good: rushing for 123.3 yards per game (11th), averaging 4.4 yards per carry (11th), -0.03 EPA per rush (10th), 26 runs that gain 10+ yards (7th), and explosive runs 16.7% (3rd).

However, there are some concerning numbers that point to struggles with consistency, including:

Rushing DVOA: 26th

Rushing success rate: 38.7% (20th)

Stuffed rate: 20% (26th)

Adjusted line yards: 3.64 (27th)

The Dolphins will want to establish their rushing attack against the Lions, and Detroit will need to match that downhill physicality. It wouldn’t be surprising to see the Lions spend a lot of time in base early as both teams work to control the trenches. Expect seven and eight defenders in the box pre-snap, and a situational spy to track Willis is likely.

With changes coming to the Lions’ linebacker roles, Detroit will need Derrick Barnes, Trevor Nowaske, and Malcolm Rodriguez to elevate their games and keep the explosive runs in check.

Prediction 4: Lions pass rushers get after Willis

If the Dolphins can establish the run, they do a nice job of running play-action behind it and finding success. But that’s not always an option for Miami’s offense, and the inconsistencies in the run game have forced Willis to create opportunities on his own.

Willis is talented—we saw that in Green Bay—comfortable passing from the pocket, and able to extend plays by escaping outside. But with limited support, he holds onto the ball too long, takes sacks, or misses his targets because his accuracy gets loose/inconsistent on the run. Miami’s offensive line is average at best (see below) and doesn’t hold up well against pressure, and while the Dolphins receivers have unique skills, they lack a true playmaker and currently rely on two rookies—Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell—in starting wide receiver roles.

As a result, Miami’s passing offense numbers are near the bottom of the league:

Pass yards per game: 166.7 (30th)

Pass yards per play: 6.9 (20th)

EPA per pass: -0.16 (24th)

Explosive passes: 24th

Willis EPA per dropback: -0.10 (27th)

Willis EPA per pressure: -0.70 (36th)

Pressures rate allowed: 43.2% (31st)

Sack rate allowed: 10.3% (31st)

The Lions would benefit by giving Willis no relief. Entering this game, the Lions have registered 116 pressures (5th best), a 35.8% pressure rate (17th), 24 sacks (third most), and a 7.4% sack rate (7th). Defense has found success against the Dolphins by rushing four and sending the blitz, so the Lions should have options to create pressure; they just need to find the right elixir to disrupt Willis.

Wonnum is still in the NFL’s concussion protocol, and while he still has a chance to pass the protocols this week, his lack of return to practice suggests he is a bit further back than hoped.

No updates on Campbell since Wednesday.

Reed said he was in a good spot in his post-game media availability last Sunday, so his absence from practice could mean his injury was worse than he realized or that the team is giving the veteran extra time to be ready. We’ll find out more on Friday.

Limited practice

St. Brown got a little banged up in Week 7, but it’s rare to see him scale back even a little, so it’s not surprising that he was back on the practice field this week, and expectations are that he is on track to play against the Dolphins.

In the locker room on Thursday, St. Brown said he was injured on his non-touchdown catch (the play that was overturned), but added, “I’m a little banged up, but I’ll be alright.”

Joseph is expanding his practice exposure this week, but the team is not going to rush him back, and Campbell has already said they don’t plan to activate him this week. michigan.headline: Friday Discussion: Is the Michigan-MSU football rivalry dead?
michigan.body:
The Michigan Wolverines host the Michigan State Spartans tomorrow night in the latest installment of the battle for the Paul Bunyan Trophy.

I thought I’d get the headline out of the way early since not many people know the game is even going on. In a year in which both Pat Fitzgerald and Kyle Whittingham are having disastrous starts to their tenures at their respective schools, the battle for Paul Bunyan certainly feels like an afterthought.

With the advent of the 24-team College Football Playoff and the death of conference championship games, rivalry games seem to be on the hot seat in college football. Is the Michigan vs. Michigan State football rivalry already dead, or is this simply a down year because of the lack of success by both teams?

Historically, Michigan State has been Michigan’s second-biggest rival behind archenemy Ohio State. However, it has certainly been the chippiest rivalry of the bunch. Between the tunnel assault by MSU, Mike Hart’s little brother comments, Devin Bush’s field stomping, and Trouble With The Snap, the drama has always been apparent. Things have been calmer in recent years in large part due to the lack of competition.

The Wolverines have won the last four MSU matchups and six of the last eight. All the while, the Spartans have cycled through Mel Tucker, Jonathan Smith, and now have Fitzgerald. Things could certainly re-escalate if Fitzgerald can right the ship, but that appears a long way off.

The larger point in this discussion circles around the 24-team CFP. It’s been discussed ad nauseam the affects that CFP expansion may or may not have on The Game. However, not many people have discussed the Michigan-Michigan State rivalry. How will the CFP affect it moving forward?

For one, a loss isn’t nearly as devastating as it used to be. In a 24-team field, teams could survive three or even four losses and still make it in. From a Michigan perspective, while a loss to the Spartans would be annoying, it would no longer doom the entire season. On the flip side, an upset win over your rival, while still fun, wouldn’t hit quite the same if your rival still made the CFP. Michigan fans know this well, as the Wolverines knocked off the Buckeyes in Columbus in 2024 before Ohio State went on to win the National Championship.

In my opinion, we are heading in the direction where Michigan vs. Michigan State is just another game. However, I could very well be proven wrong. We know that the vitriol and hatred from MSU towards Michigan is second to none. Does a rivalry like this one have more staying power than other, more on-field based rivalries? Are geographic rivalries at an advantage or a disadvantage in the 24-team playoff era?

Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.

michigan.headline: Michigan Mailbag: Does Kyle Whittingham understand the importance of the MSU game?
michigan.body:
Kyle Whittingham, the head coach of the Michigan Wolverines, reacts during an NCAA football game at SHI Stadium in Piscataway, United States, on October 31, 2026. (Photo by Dan Squicciarini/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images

The Michigan Football program is coming off a win against Rutgers. While it looked touch-and-go at times, the offense managed enough points to help the defense out and win the game. The defense struggled a bit for the first time all year, giving up a handful of big plays to a Rutgers offense that just didn’t have much to work with. A win is something we’ll take, and the Wolverines now sit at 5-3 with four games remaining.

Now, it’s time for the team to turn its attention to the first major rivalry game of the season and the first for head coach Kyle Whittingham. We asked you to post your questions ahead of the MSU game in The Feed, so let’s get right to them.

On the defense’s response after last week

Hopefully well. We all probably expected the defense to give up fewer points to Rutgers, but if you want to look on the bright side, at least they have some areas to fix heading into this week’s game.

The defense has been elite, but several players struggled while we had some of the best players on the sidelines last week. Hopefully we get some good news on the injury front, too — while the coaches said they expect Dom Nichols and John Henry Daley to play, they’re still listed as questionable on the availability report. Having Rod Moore dealing with an injury has also been an issue for the secondary.

To actually answer your question, Michigan will need to limit its penalties. The Michigan State rivalry can get heated, and playing hard without focus could lead to some silly penalties that keep Michigan State’s offense on the field. If they can attack with intensity and make some tackles, Michigan’s defense should look fine again.

On Kyle Whittingham

Maybe I’m in the minority, but I don’t think there’s any chance Michigan moves on from Whittingham even if he were to lose out. At this point, it doesn’t feel like there’s much he can do to get people back on his side. While wins over Ohio State and UCLA will certainly help us feel better, some of the complaints against Whittingham are bigger than just his loss column. The calls for his job will probably die down, but if he doesn’t make some changes to his offensive staff, I don’t think many people will be excited heading into next season.

On the Michigan State rivalry

It sounds like people are getting Whittingham up to speed on the Michigan State rivalry, but a few of his statements didn’t sound super promising this week. He’s been pointing out this isn’t Michigan’s biggest rivalry game. While that’s a fun point to make with family at the dinner table around the holidays, I’m not the biggest fan of Michigan’s head coach telling everyone it’s Michigan State’s Super Bowl.

MSU’s new head coach Pat Fitzgerald knows what this game means to his fans. He also knows what it looks like to prepare for games in the Big Ten. It feels like it could be a recipe for disaster on Saturday. This could also be me acting overdramatic. I guess we’ll find out tomorrow.

Let’s keep the conversation going in the comments. Post your thoughts below!

msu.headline: Getting To Know The Enemy: 6Qs About The um wolverines
msu.body:
Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham watches practice at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor ahead of the game between Michigan and Oklahoma on Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

Happy Thursday, TOC Nation.  This column has been away for a few weeks with a bye last week and the game against UCLA before that, which does not have an SB Nation site.  But we are back for our in-state hate game.  I sat down with Von Lozon of Maize N Brew for a quick look at this weekend’s opponent.  Let’s see what he had to say.

The Only Colors: UM is in the first year under head coach Kyle Whittingham. Did that hire take you by surprise? Aside from any surprise, what were your thoughts on the hire? What were your expectations for this season in terms of performance and record?

Von Lozon:  I wasn’t surprised, but I was skeptical of the hire simply due to his age and me wondering how much he had left in the tank. I never thought he was a bad coach or anything like that — if anything, I thought he was one of the more underrated coaches in the country — but I was a little nervous about how things would translate at Michigan and in the Big Ten. I thought this team’s ceiling heading into the year was 9-3, which they can still technically reach, but I would be incredibly shocked if that happened.

TOC: Your season opener came down to a famously controversial ending. I won’t ask you for your thoughts on how that played out. But I would like to know how much panic you had after that first game? After that 1st game, UM was expected to lose their 2nd game against Oklahoma. How did that win reshape your expectations?

VL: Given my offseason skepticism, I was really worried following the WMU game. But then the Wolverines beat Oklahoma the very next week and I was thinking to myself, “Okay, maybe that is more of what we should expect.” And then the next week, Michigan was in a first-half dog fight against UTEP, so at that point, I knew this would be a team that plays up (and down) to its competition. That has continued every week all season, as the only game that wasn’t a one-score affair was that UTEP game. Needless to say, it’s been a roller coaster of a year for Michigan.

TOC: Whittingham has made a switch at QB, with Tommy Carr taking over a couple games ago as the starter. What do you think went wrong with Bryce Underwood? Should the switch have been made sooner? What do you like about Carr’s game that makes him better than Underwood?

VL: It’s a really curious case, right? Underwood flashed his potential at times during his freshman season, but he looked even more lost this year before the coaching staff made the change. It’s interesting, especially considering all the reports coming out of fall camp were that Underwood had improved under the new coaching staff’s direction and should take a sophomore leap. But his freshman tendencies (staring down one receiver, bailing out of the pocket too soon, etc.) came back to haunt him this season, resulting in far too many negative plays and turnovers.

I do think the switch should have been made during the game at Minnesota, but admittedly, that would have been a really tough spot to put a freshman quarterback in the game for the first time. The thing I like so far about Carr is his poise. He hasn’t let anything phase him too much yet — even though he struggled at the start of the Indiana game with a couple of turnovers, he kept his head down, kept working and eventually put Michigan in a good position to win (thanks a lot, Jason Beck!).

TOC: Tell us about the Wolverine defense. What is the base formation? What level of the D is the best? What player do the MSU coaches most need to game plan for?

VL: The defense is by far the best part of this football team. Jay Hill runs a true 4-3 defensive scheme with the linebackers playing off the ball. The wrinkle is that one of the linebackers can be a bit of a hybrid player at times. Depending on the call, that linebacker can be up on the line of scrimmage setting the edge or dropping into the box. It gives Michigan’s defense some flexibility without needing to change personnel. Look for Chase Taylor (No. 4), who has been in this role quite a bit this year, as well as MIKE linebacker Troy Bowles (No. 18).
The best level of the defense is the defensive line. Michigan can rotate edge rushers like John Henry Daley, Dom Nichols, Nate Marshall, Benny Patterson III, and true freshmen Tariq Boney and Carter Meadows without a real drop-off. The interior group of Trey Pierce, Enow Etta and Jonah Lea’ea has been solid as well. That depth lets them stay fresh and keep the pressure on for four quarters.

The player MSU needs to game plan for is Daley. He missed last week’s game due to an injury, but he is expected to play this weekend. He leads the team in sacks (4) and also has 6.5 tackles for loss. When he has been on the field, he has been Michigan’s best edge rusher. Nichols is right behind him, and the two of them together are why the defense can get to the quarterback so often without blitzing.

TOC: Fill in the blank: UM will win if ___________.  UM will lose if ___________.

VL: U-M will win if they avoid turning the ball over, run the ball well (AKA: go on long drives that drain the clock), and score touchdowns, not field goals, in the red zone.

U-M will lose if they turn the ball over, give up some explosive plays to MSU’s offense (much like vs Rutgers last week), and take MSU lightly. On that last point, I’m a little worried these guys don’t really know a whole lot about this rivalry. Kyle Whittingham has said multiple times that this game is important, but it isn’t the most important rivalry game Michigan has. Savion Hiter said all he knows about this game is that the rivalry is “dirty.” I really have not enjoyed hearing the things that some of these guys have said throughout the week, so I really, really hope Michigan doesn’t take MSU for granted.

TOC: Predict the final score.

VL: Michigan 20, Michigan State 17.

msu.headline: HATE WEEK- Hate: a Michigan State-Michigan History
msu.body:
Editor’s Note: This is an older post from 2011 that has been updated in the sole instance of the series record through 2025, but remains otherwise unchanged. We are placing it back on the frontpage in 2026 ahead of the Michigan State vs. um game as it remains a fan favorite here at The Only Colors.

—

Author’s note: Yup, this is a long one. It gets a little sweary, but nothing too bad.

For those unfamiliar with our background, at different times MSU was known as M.A.C. (Michigan Agricultural College) and MSC (Michigan State College), as our size and mission grew.

This is only tangentially about football, but very much about the rivalry swirling about our game for Paul Bunyan. Many of you have probably heard of most of these claims before (they float around message boards, and are mostly up on Wikipedia), but I’ve attempted here to bring what’d I earlier heard and read as rumors into the realm of fact, or at least informed deduction, with some citation, quotes of reliable sources, and attempts at humor. Enjoy.

“So, what’s the deal with you guys?”

It’s been called an inferiority complex. It’s been called jealousy. Mike Hart infamously labeled us “Little Brother.” Michigan State University does not like the University of Michigan. But why?

Having two major institutions in the same state and conference is a good start, as closeness and familiarity almost always breed contempt (Notre Dame chops Indiana three ways, in addition to Indiana and Purdue, and Northwestern has typically never put the focus on athletics to really bother Illinois until recently). A football rivalry first dominated by one side before the second half of the 20th century, that then turned pretty close in more recent times (before the 2026 matchup, the record stands at 42-29-2 UM since the Paul Bunyan Trophy was established in 1953, 10-9 MSU since 2007 when Mark Dantonio took over), with several epic and controversial games in the past decade, has helped build animosity. The biggest cheating scandal in NCAA history, perpetuated with the knowledge and consent of U of M officials, held back MSU’s basketball progress for at least a decade, hurt a great coach’s legacy in Jud Heathcote, and only increased the dislike from MSU fans. And as Coach Dantonio and Mark Hollis have each remarked several times, you’re either blue or green in this state.

But few of these criteria are unique to MSU-UM (except, I must emphasize, the MASSIVE, MASSIVE AMOUNTS OF CHEATING DONE BY THE FAB FIVE AND OTHER MEMBERS OF UM BASKETBALL IN THE ’80s AND ’90s). Rivalries are fairly common among college teams. Everyone has a rival; every school has a school (or three) they hate, at least in theory.

But I’d argue what I and scores of other Spartan fans feel towards University of Michigan Ann Arbor is something a little different. It’s hate with a long history behind it, the type of history only the best of rivalries can claim, one that folds in and out of athletics, academia, and other bad blood*. A story with likable good guys and hate-able villains that takes the whole rivalry one step further for fans of the green and white (and black and bronze).

The University of Michigan, tried, for a long time, to wrap its hands around the neck of our university at nearly every turn, displaying the type of arrogance, elitism, and anti-competitive policies of subterfuge and sabotage that have made the university reviled throughout all of the Big Ten.

*For example, we don’t touch the KU-Mizzou rivalry, the aptly named Border War, which literally started during a conflict, the Civil War, when fights broke out between Missouri and Kansas over whether the state would be free or slave, when it joined the Union. Missouri, to my knowledge is one of the few universities that can claim it raided and set fire to its rival’s university town (Lawrence) during a major massacre (Though West Virginia University counters said claims, arguing that it too has set a university town on fire, while noting that said town is Morgantown)

Opposition to our very creation

Our story begins over a century and a half ago in the 1850s. The state of Michigan had a big problem: inferior agriculture. In 1837, a law was passed upgrading the state’s premier university, which, of course, was the University of Michigan, to its current location in Ann Arbor. U of M, which was already eager, willing, and able to train the state’s new lawyers, doctors, and theologians, also promised that, “there shall be a department of agriculture, with competent instructors…” that would study the theory, physiology, chemistry, and practice of farming and agriculture. (Kuhn, 1955 pg. 1)

As you might guess, over the following dozen years, the University of Michigan absolutely did not do this, at the very least not to the quantity or quality they promised. We can prove this, not only with oratorical record (Kuhn quotes E.H. Lothrup, the speaker at the first Michigan state fair, as pleading for an agricultural institution that would train hundreds of men each year, not just the 20 to 30 that the University of Michigan was graduating, in 1849), but with agricultural data and food production decisions at the time (Kuhn notes wheat yields had declined, railroads had threatened Michigan’s livestock farmers with competition from the East, and that the lure of California and the American West might depopulate Michigan of its rural farmers unless things improved). (Kuhn, 1955 pg. 2)

Rising to this call for action was the Michigan State Agricultural Society. Several sources of revenue were sought, but each ran into roadblocks. Private funding wasn’t available, the state government was too poor to assist, and the average taxpayer too poor to tax for the cash.

Seeing that the Wolverines weren’t going to solve the problem and that the state didn’t have the money to start a new college on its own, the state made the first petition to the national Congress that would eventually result in the Morrill Act of 1862 being passed. (Kuhn, 1955 pg. 7)

But that wasn’t for 12 more years. And here in 1850, they had a problem on their hands now. So the group and their allies included a clause in Michigan’s second Constitution, which read simply: “The Legislature shall… as soon as practicable, provide for the establishment of an Agricultural School.” The money wasn’t there yet. But there was a gift of land of about 1,400 acres of so-called Salt Spring Lands for whatever institution chose to form the agricultural school. (Kuhn, pg. 5-6)

A floundering, cash-strapped ancestor to what is now Michigan State University, then based in Ypsilanti, jumped at this opportunity for land. So too did the University of Michigan, leaping into half-assed action like the roommate late on rent for four straight months, but promising that he’ll get it to you this time bro. He promises. (Kuhn, 1955, pg. 7)

Both institutions sent proposals to the state legislature, who couldn’t decide and took a wait-and-see approach. So each institution then set up competing agricultural programs, but the school in Ypsilanti didn’t have the size, and the University in Ann Arbor lacked the staff, commitment, and audience to maintain their agricultural program, folding it after only a little over a year. (Kuhn, 1955, pg 7)

After these failed bids, it was pretty clear to the head honchos of Michigan agriculture that they needed an exclusive, separate agricultural institution to perform the function needed and guaranteed by the state constitution. (Kuhn 1955, pg 8)

Standing in the way was Michigan president and historical Wolverine shithead Henry P. Tappan, a man who made a career out of opposing any threat to his university’s monolithic control of higher education in the state of Michigan (also, as it happens, a man far too cultured to take a stance on the slavery question, and, I kid you not, a man who basically said that people could not get intoxicated from drinking wine. That’s a century-and-a-half old buttress holding up U of M’s wine-and-cheese-crowd reputation, folks) Tappan was clear, when it came to an Agricultural College, it was in Ann Arbor, or nowhere. The State Legislature, under the watchful eye of “friend of MSU” John C. Holmes and his allies, was equally clear: “Fuck off, Wolverines.” The Agricultural College of Michigan was established, separate from the U of M. (Kuhn, 1955 pg. 8-9)

But the college wasn’t in the clear yet. Several provisions in the bill looked to kneecap the institution, some coming from self-interested state senators, some undoubtedly coming from Tappan’s faction, the most painful of which was a change from Holmes’ recommendation of authorizing the M.A.C. $25 with which to purchase each acre of land, to only authorizing $15 per acre, a reduction that drastically reduced the quality of land available. As Kuhn puts it, this was “dooming the college to commence in the forest,” hardly suitable farmland for an agricultural institution! (Kuhn, 1955 pg. 10-11)

The second stipulation ordered that the College be established within 10 miles of Lansing, something that doesn’t seem like a big deal now, but was considerably tougher when the land 10 miles outside of Lansing was a road-less, infrastructure-less wild, functionally ruled by undergrowth, bears, and six-foot-long mosquitoes that would often carry away small children [citation needed]. (Kuhn, 1955 pg 10)

But as tough as things were, what would eventually become MSU was established, and though it struggled and pushed its way through its first half a decade of existence, it had shown that it wasn’t going to back down to Ann Arbor. All the school needed was a big break. And the opportunity for that break arrived, from the aforementioned Morrill Act, in 1862.

Attempted theft of our Morrill Grant, destruction of our independence

President Lincoln and the U.S. Congress recognized that the nation’s various agricultural institutions, like M.A.C., needed the type of boost other public schools had gotten from the government. With this in mind, they passed the Morrill Act, which, as Kuhn writes, “…gave to agricultural colleges a promise of permanence which had been lacking previously.” (Kuhn, 1955, pg 71)

The Morrill Act offered a massive grant of land, pretty good land, to one institution in each state. Given its purpose and the letter of the law, it was to be available for schools where “the leading object shall be, without excluding other scientific and classical studies… to teach such branches of learning as are related to agriculture and the agricultural arts…” M.A.C. administrators, teachers, and students, had to be ecstatic. That was them! It was right in the curriculum, the purpose, heck, the name! They were finally going to get some help and be able to do what they were established to do. (Kuhn, 1955, pg. 71-75)

As you might expect, the University of Michigan, now having pissed all over us for half a dozen years now, saw a clear opportunity for R. Kelly levels of degrading urination.

“Well, there’s no way in hell we’re going to get that Morrill money allocated to us,” they correctly surmised, probably while stroking comically evil mustaches, “Unlesssssss…”

“A merger.” They proposed. “We should merge M.A.C. into the U of M system.”

They would transfer agricultural education to Ann Arbor, and the land from the Morrill land would be assigned to the University of Michigan. (Kuhn, 1955 pg 76-77)

“Why?” people asked.

“Shut up,” they responded, trying to hide the places on their plan where they’d been doodling themselves carrying big bags of money. If they couldn’t stop M.A.C. from getting established, and if they couldn’t stop it from getting the Morrill money, they could steal it without doing much more work than lobbying legislators. Apparently, in the U of M administrator’s version of the “The Little Red Hen,” all of the farm animals who didn’t do any work making the cake sneak in and gobble the cake all up, after the hen leaves the room.

The committee, probably rightfully seeing that merging the colleges was not cost-effective or educationally preferable, decided to award M.A.C. the land grant in 1863. This, of course, did not stop the University of Michigan from try, try, trying again and re-introducing the merger proposal on three more occasions in 1865, 1867, and 1869. Kuhn writes, “Even though they failed of passage, their following was numerous enough to defeat all proposed building appropriations” to M.A.C. If U of M could not stop our creation, or steal our land grant, they would do their damnedest to strangle our funding. The College’s single residency hall was subject to such crowding that half of a new year’s admissions applications were denied (think of how much USNWR would like us with that kind of rejection rate!) (Kuhn 1955, pg. 78)

But despite their best efforts (including actually trying to induce our school president into approving the merger with an offer “that his friends would try to find him [Abbott] a position in the University [of Michigan] if the merger succeeded,” the type of “join us, and we can rule the galaxy together!” offer I only thought bad guys made in movies), they failed. In 1869, M.A.C. at last fought off the obstructionism and was finally appropriated funding for a new dormitory. (Kuhn, 1955 pg 78-81)

Attempted theft of our forestry program

There was a period of peace between the universities for a number of years, but like a kleptomaniac who just can’t help himself, within half a century, they were back to old tricks. This one is probably less openly dickish than the other attempts by Michigan to steal our programs, as it at least pays some respect to us first, and admits that we’re better than them at something, before trying to take credit for it. Due to its surrounding forests, in the early 1900’s M.A.C.’s undergraduate forestry program was producing practical, effective, foresters, in sharp contrast to the theoretically skilled, but practically unprepared, graduates of graduate-level forestry programs at places like Cornell, Michigan or Yale. A U of M professor wrote a letter to the president of our forestry program complimenting it and its methods. (Widder 2005 pg 162-163)

Then, like clockwork, proposals were made that either one program or the other should drop its forestry program in the unification, either M.A.C. its undergraduate program, or U of M its graduate. (Widder 2005 pg. 164)

Prominent forest expert and Yale grad Gifford Pinchot weighed in on the side of U of M and argued M.A.C. should drop its undergraduate program, saying that moving forestry to the University of Michigan would be “an immense advantage to the progress of forestry in Michigan” and that moving forestry to M.A.C. would be “destructive.” This move isn’t as villainous as some other moves, particularly if, as proponents argued, such a move would have a net positive effect on American forestry knowledge. But, as it turned out, contra to the thinking of Mr. Pinchot, an undergraduate program was both feasible and effective, training good foresters as well as fulfilling the goals of our land grant background.

The entire episode smacks of an arrogant attitude — that if MSU is better than Michigan, Yale, and Cornell at a field of study, then something is wrong with the world. (Widder, 2005 pg 164)

Professor is part of U of M sleeper cell (not really … maybe), is sort of traitor to MSU

W.J. Beal graduated with degrees from the University of Michigan and Harvard. He then proceeded to spend most of his career teaching botany at M.A.C. and generally did various cool-dude things, like setting up MSU’s famous botanic garden, curating for our museum, and doing strong and important research in his field of study. He was also kind of a Benedict Arnold. (Widder 2005 pg 62)

One day in 1914, he must have heard his activation code phrase, because he proposed (again!) that M.A.C. be rolled up into the Michigan system to “spare the university [of Michigan] from duplicating courses offered at M.A.C.” (Widder 2005 pg 70-71)

Nearly everyone, including the presidents of M.A.C. and U of M, said, “WTF guy?” A member of the State Agriculture Board noted that Beal had probably confused the college’s mission as promoting and producing agricultural scientists (like, well, Beal) and not training farmers. Both were probably wrong, as the college existed to train both, and its independence was key to doing so. The two colleges wisely shot down Beal’s bizarre proposal. (Widder 2005 pg 71-72)

Attempted theft of our engineering program

Of course, that didn’t stop the Wolverines from trying to lift other fields. Yeah, this again. In this case, it’s the Wolverines showing a slimy willingness to take advantage of misfortune at M.A.C.

In 1916, a fire (though zero evidence indicates involvement of a Michigan Man arsonist, I would not be surprised at this point) destroyed the college’s engineering building and much of its engineering equipment. After failing in bids to acquire our engineering department in 1913 and 1915, Wolverines saw now as a good (and by good, I mean dickish) time to strike. (Kuhn, 1955 pg. 266-267)

Like Crassus sending his early fire brigades to burning Roman buildings, they were willing to “help” us in our time of pain. “Real shame about your engineering program,” seemed to be the line, “We, uh, wouldn’t mind taking it off your hands for you.”

Then president of the college, Frank Kedzie, rallied the engineering students and faculty, some of whom had escaped from the still-smoldering remains of the old engineering building, and, in a moment of Churchillian swagger before Churchill was Churchill, is quoted by Kuhn to have said, “It is up to you men to keep a stiff upper lip. It lies with you as to whether or not the engineering department will live.” (Kuhn, 1955 pg. 267)

Immediately, the students and teachers set about to utilizing other rooms in the campus to continue their instruction. Meanwhile, Kedzie contacted Lansing automaker Ransom E. Olds (winner of the 1916 cool name award), and basically said, “Remember that time we talked about you getting a building with your name on it? Now would be a real, real, good time to make that a reality.” Olds’ agreed and donated $100,000 to build a new engineering building. Kuhn writes, “Just as the construction of Williams Hall in 1869 ended a fight to move agriculture to the University [of Michigan], so the construction of Olds Hall in 1916 ended the fight to move engineering.”

With this, our existence and independence was finally secured from the ambitions of our rivals. But what of our further prominence?

Lack of support for MSC to the Big Ten

In football, despite the great work of Biggie Munn, football was being held back. David Thomas writes that President of MSC John Hannah thought the problem was, “weak schedules; beating Grinnell, Carnegie Tech, Wayne State, and Alma created little excitement in national football circles. And, of course, potential recruits tended to choose colleges that scheduled games against elite programs. Moreover, the top schools that agreed to play MSC often insisted on playing the games at home, forcing the Spartans continually to play in front of hostile crowds. Prior to 1947, for example, 29 of Michigan State’s 33 varsity games against the University of Michigan took place in Ann Arbor.” (Thomas, 2007)

This could be fixed by joining the Big Ten (also known as the Western Conference), and when the University of Chicago dropped athletics to cut the Big Ten to the Big Nine, MSU had a chance to get in. (Thomas 2007)

Did U of M oppose this move on MSC’s part? It’s tricky. There seemed to be some support from the president of the university, Alexander Ruthven, who noted strategically in a letter to Hannah, that despite his support (or at least lack of opposition), “You know, I am sure, that the presidents have absolutely no voice in determining the policies of the conference except as we may occasionally insist that we will not go along with some policy.” He was not as involved in athletic decisions like conference alignment.

Thomas notes another avenue of support from a Wolverine. “The president of the University of Michigan Alumni Club of Lansing, Dr. Maurice C. Loree, wrote to Hannah that his group ‘heartily endorse[d] Michigan State College as a Member of the Big Ten Conference and as evidence of that support we are attaching hereto a copy of a formal resolution we have sent to the officials of the University of Michigan.'” Though, Loree too, of course, was not the power behind the decision at U of M. (Thomas 2007)

As evidence of Michigan’s typical role of obstructionist and saboteur, Thomas writes of the general undecurrent behind the anti-MSC vibe from U of M that undercut previous acts of support, “Despite Ruthven’s apparent support a few years earlier, the University of Michigan opposed having an in-state school join the conference, believing that the UM’s intrastate dominance would be curtailed,” as well as President Hannah’s later thoughts on the ordeal, “We knew from the beginning that there would be no friendly consideration of Michigan State’s cause by the Big Ten if the University of Michigan had its way. We anticipated that Ann Arbor would be unfriendly and critical and obstructive, and that is exactly what they were.” (Thomas 2007)

When Hannah wrote to then-Michigan Big Ten Faculty Representative Ralph Aigler to get an update on U of M’s thoughts to MSC’s admission status, he got the “Yeah, I don’t think so” reply from Aigler: “There was … no definite vote on your application. When the matter came before the Faculty Representatives, I made a statement to the effect that I hoped the Conference would see its way clear to elect Michigan State, but I did not press for a vote, realizing that the temper of the group was to approve the Directors’ recommendation [that no change be made in membership]. I thought it was better to leave the matter more or less in suspense. What, if anything, it may have had to do with the general attitude, I cannot say, but it was not uncommon to hear a remark to the effect that a man or woman ought not to remarry until a decent interval has elapsed after the spouse’s death. … After a little more time has gone by, one will be able to tell better what the long range disposition of the group is.” (Thomas 2007)

So what about the vote? We obviously were ultimately admitted. But did Michigan vote for, or against, our application? Well, it’s unclear here again. But I have a guess.

A Lansing State Journal writer noted, “If there is a vote taken and it’s favorable, you can be very sure that it will be announced as a unanimous one. There will be some kind words spoken. If there is a negative result (and we have no way of knowing if the case will actually be voted upon at all!) there will be no comment.” When the vote was announced and MSC was accepted (Hurray!) it was indeed announced as a 9-0 unanimous vote. I repeat, announced. Maybe it really was unanimous. But given Hannah’s comments, evidence at the time, and the general swirl of rumors since, I’m inclined to believe that had Michigan been the swing vote or the vote was in favor of voting against us, the Wolverines almost certainly would have rejected us (Michigan’s recent back stab of Nebraska in the AAU does nothing to damper this suspicion). The fact that they didn’t want to be the only, or one of the few, no votes, combined with pressure from the Big Ten, probably meant even if they had wanted to vote no (or did vote no) it wouldn’t show up in the news reports of the result, for reasons of face and faux unity. (Thomas 2007)

Opposition to our name change to Michigan State University

In 1954, MSC sent a request to the legislature requesting our name be changed to Michigan State University. The argument here was pretty simple: we’d been functionally operating as a university since the 1930s and most of the other land-grant institutions had already been granted university status. In fact, we’d tried twice before, in 1949 and 1951, and failed. But we’d grown since WWII and had the type of athletic and academic success that should have helped our reputation and sealed the name change. Doesn’t seem like that big a deal, right? (Thomas 2008 pg 251-252)

Wrong. The University of Michigan freaked. The U of M board of regents met a month later and gave as reasons to why we shouldn’t get to change our name to MSU (I shit you not): “A name change would confuse the identity of the institutions… it would be unconstitutional because both the University of Michigan and Michigan State College names were embedded in the Michigan constitution, and that it would lead to (Heck: U of M’s favorite anti-competition excuse) duplication of programs.” LOL, I mean, it reads like satire. (Thomas, 2008 pg 252)

It would be just a hilarious footnote in their regime of stabs at our legitimacy, except that their stupid, spiteful bitching delayed the name change for about half a year, until the Michigan Congress and government finally got done laughing their asses off at UM’s crappy arguments and approved the name change in a landslide. (Thomas 2008, pg 252-258)

To sum it up

The story behind MSU-UM goes beyond the football field, or the basketball court, to something more raw. If Michigan had their way over the years, MSU would either not exist, be severely limited, or be a lobotomized satellite under their umbrella.

It’s not all about the sports teams (though that certainly doesn’t help matters). It isn’t even about the obvious condescension. It’s the century of open hostility and behind-the-scenes sabotage coming from Ann Arbor. The use of political levers and influence in an attempt to keep us down, as though education was a zero-sum game. Maybe this has happened to other schools, but here at MSU, no other program has as consistently, or systemically, tried to undermine our status as an educational institution and athletic program. In the past, they tried to crush my school under their boot heel and probably would have kept trying if we hadn’t gotten too good, and too big, for them to pick on anymore.

All we originally wanted to do was fill a gap. Do the work U of M wasn’t doing, educate the students U of M wasn’t teaching. It’s what we still do. And eventually, yes, we wanted to contribute to the fields that U of M was traditionally strong in too, and become well-rounded and nationally respected. And we’ve done that too. But we’ve had to do it with the University of Michigan throwing garbage and rocks at us, every step of the way.

And that’s a shame, because the University of Michigan Ann Arbor, is, and always has been, a good enough school athletically, and academically, to not need to resort to this type of action. Your school is really good. You make and discover and teach valuable things. I just wish that could have been enough for you. We were probably always going to be rivals, but it could have been friendly, at least off the playing fields. I guess fair competition was always a little too risky for the Wolverines, so instead, they tried to pull the plug on, or take credit for, various Spartans’ hard work, time after time. You don’t get to try to bury something that’s important to us and then expect us to shrug it off, though they’ll probably never understand that.

So, yeah, it’ s sort of personal. You thought we’d forget?

Fortunately, the story comes complete with a happy ending. They tried to kill us, but they couldn’t. Spartans, so the legends go, don’t die easily. We were too smart, too tough, too, well, good. And now, as the past half century has shown, we’re done having to deal with the sort of nonsense chronicled in this piece. We’re here to stay, free from this sort of petty sniping, political maneuvering, and constant second-guessing. So don’t forget the heroes and villains of this piece. Hate, because for many reasons hate has been earned, but also, be happy. Be happy because we beat the odds and that means so many good things, for so many good people.

Ultimately, MSU is a success story. Our school has grown from its simple roots to a university where students can feasibly claim they receive an education among the best in the country, while still fulfilling its goals to serve a large cross-section of students from around the country, and the globe. That’s pretty cool. And, hey, the sports aren’t too bad either.

Bibliography

-Kuhn, Madison, 1955. ‘Michigan State: The First Hundred Years 1985-1955’ published by: Michigan State University Press

-Thomas, David. 2008. ‘Michigan State College’ published by: Michigan State University Press

-Thomas, David, 2007. ‘How MSU became a member of the Big Ten Conference’ MSU Alumni Association Magazine, http://alumni.msu.edu/magazine/article.cfm?id=1154

-Widder, Keith, 2005. ‘Michigan Agricultural College’, published by: Michigan State University Press

msu.headline: Michigan State Football: Show Me the NIL Money
msu.body:
Michigan State Athletic Director Dan Bartholomae, left, talks with football coach Pat Fitzgerald after the Spartans win over Toledo on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, at Spartan Stadium in East Lansing. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

With Michigan State enjoying a much-needed bye week, I’m taking a break from the usual Film Room breakdown. After weeks of watching missed blocks, blown assignments, turnovers and just about every other way to lose a football game, I think we’ve all earned a week off. My eyes certainly have.

Instead, let’s talk about money. Specifically, how much Michigan State is reportedly spending on its football roster and how that compares with the rest of the Big Ten. Between NIL, the transfer portal and revenue sharing, college football has become an expensive business. Several estimates value Michigan State’s roster at around $23 million this season. That’s a lot of money, but apparently not in the Big Ten, where it puts the Spartans in the bottom half of the conference.

So, are the Spartans spending enough to compete? Are they getting enough out of the resources they already have? And with the Big Ten adopting new rules governing athlete compensation, what will it cost to turn Michigan State back into a competitive football program?

What Is Michigan State Actually Spending?

Trying to figure out how much college football teams spend on their rosters is like splitting a dinner bill with 18 people. Nobody agrees on the numbers and everyone claims they paid their share.

Unlike professional sports, there’s no public salary sheet showing what every player makes. Fortunately, several outlets have taken a crack at estimating Michigan State’s 2026 roster. In September, ⁠The Athletic estimated MSU’s football budget between $21 million and $25 million, ranking the Spartans 11th among 18 Big Ten programs.

⁠The NIL Standard values Michigan State at $23 million, also 11th in the conference and $6.5 million below its estimated Big Ten average of $29.5 million. ⁠The Sideline arrives at the same $23 million figure, ranking MSU 37th nationally among the programs it tracks. Meanwhile, ⁠StickToTheModel uses its own player valuation model, with estimates that vary depending on how the roster is calculated.

The individual player estimates below show just how much these valuations can vary depending on who’s doing the math. The NIL Standard values Alessio Milivojevic at approximately $1.42 million, followed by offensive tackle Ben Murawski at $1.27 million and edge rusher Kenny Soares Jr. at $1.06 million. Meanwhile, StickToTheModel puts Milivojevic closer to $1 million, a difference of more than $400,000. It also has Ben Roberts leading Michigan State’s roster at $1.4 million. Keep in mind, these are estimated NIL values, not confirmed earnings, and the two models clearly don’t agree on what everyone is worth.

None of these figures represents a confirmed university payroll, and the models don’t necessarily measure the same things. Still, multiple estimates put Michigan State somewhere around $23 million.

The conference comparison below, from The Athletic, shows just how far that money goes in today’s Big Ten. Ohio State and Oregon lead the way with estimated football budgets around $50 million, while Michigan, USC and Indiana fall between $36 million and $40 million. Nebraska sits between $31 million and $35 million.

Using the midpoint of those estimates, Michigan State trails Michigan by roughly $15 million and Ohio State by nearly $29 million. That’s a pretty big gap when you’re trying to beat teams that can spend twice as much assembling their rosters. But MSU isn’t at the bottom, either. The Spartans rank ahead of several conference programs, including Illinois, Iowa, Purdue and Rutgers. More money would certainly help, but spending alone doesn’t explain everything we’ve watched on Saturdays.

The Big Ten’s New $49 Million Cap

Just when everyone was starting to understand NIL and revenue sharing, college sports decided it needed another financial rulebook.

On Oct. 28, the Big Ten announced new conference rules governing institutional involvement in athlete compensation, establishing a combined limit of approximately $49 million per school.

The framework includes a maximum of $27.5 million in third-party NIL agreements arranged through institutional involvement, alongside payments permitted under the existing House settlement. The conference also established financial penalties and other disciplinary measures for schools that violate the rules.

Importantly, that $49 million figure applies to an entire athletic department, not just football. Michigan State would have to divide those resources among football, basketball and its other sports. Athletes can still pursue legitimate independent NIL opportunities outside the institutional framework, meaning the limit doesn’t necessarily represent everything a school’s athletes could earn.

The Big Ten’s decision comes as Congress continues considering the Protect College Sports Act. In a report for Yahoo Sports, Ross Dellenger detailed how conference leaders were developing an alternative framework in case federal legislation stalled. The Big Ten has now moved forward with its own rules rather than waiting for Washington.

The timing matters. Schools need to know what financial resources they can offer before the next transfer portal opens, and Michigan State has plenty of roster decisions ahead.

Of course, establishing a spending limit doesn’t mean everyone can afford to reach it. Ohio State and Oregon already have significantly more financial resources committed to their football rosters than Michigan State, and new rules won’t magically close that gap.

That’s where Michigan State’s new athletic director comes in.

Dan Bartholomae Wants Michigan State Back in the Fight

Michigan State athletic director Dan Bartholomae has made it clear that he wants the Spartans spending like a program that expects to compete. In an ⁠Oct. 28 interview with Graham Couch of the Lansing State Journal, Bartholomae discussed increasing Michigan State’s investment in athletics, with football at the top of the priority list.

His goal is to provide programs expected to compete for championships with resources ranking in the top third of the Big Ten. Considering Michigan State currently sits 11th in estimated football spending, there’s some ground to make up. Bartholomae has also expressed a desire to reach the maximum spending level permitted under the new rules, potentially as soon as next year. That’s an ambitious goal, especially for an athletic department trying to make up years of lost ground.

As Couch points out, Bartholomae understands the skepticism surrounding Michigan State football. Fans have heard plenty about rebuilding, investing and returning to relevance. Meanwhile, the losses keep piling up. The new athletic director sees football as the financial engine for the entire department, and he’s right. Winning football brings ticket sales, donations, television exposure and plenty of other opportunities.

But getting anywhere near that $49 million institutional limit will require serious fundraising and new revenue. Pat Fitzgerald and his staff also need to know what they’ll have available before the next transfer portal opens. Bartholomae has identified where he wants Michigan State to go. Now he just needs to find the money to get there. Hopefully, finding the money proves easier than finding a few more wins on Saturdays.

My Thoughts: Spend More, Spend Smarter

I don’t think Michigan State needs to match Ohio State or Oregon dollar for dollar to become competitive again. But expecting to consistently compete near the top of the Big Ten while spending in the bottom half probably isn’t a great business plan.

Looking at the reported numbers, I’d like to see Michigan State move toward the $30 million to $35 million range for its football roster. That would put the Spartans closer to Nebraska and give the coaching staff more resources to recruit and retain talent. Of course, that’s a football roster target, not the same thing as the new $49 million institutional limit.

But money alone isn’t fixing this mess. Michigan State has already invested millions in a roster that has struggled with talent, depth and an injury list that seems to grow every Saturday. Those injuries have exposed just how thin the Spartans are at several positions. There’s only so much coaching can do when you’re running out of healthy bodies. Fitzgerald and his staff need more talent, better depth and hopefully a little better luck keeping everyone out of the training room.

I’m also concerned about keeping the young players who have shown promise. We’ve watched enough former Spartans find success elsewhere. The last thing this program needs is to become a developmental league for teams with bigger checkbooks.

I appreciate Bartholomae making football a priority, and I hope he can deliver on those promises. Michigan State should have the resources and ambition to compete with the better programs in this conference. But at some point, the talk about investments, rebuilding and the future needs to turn into wins on Saturdays.

Money can’t buy happiness, and apparently $23 million can’t buy a winning record in East Lansing. But in today’s college football, a bigger checkbook certainly helps. The trick is finding players worth paying and coaches who can get the most out of them.

Now I want to hear from you, Spartan fans. What’s the magic number? Is $30 million to $35 million enough to get Michigan State back in the Big Ten race, or does it take $40 million or more? And is spending more really the answer, or is spending smarter just as important? Let me know what you think in the comments.
